#3473. New Scientific Analysis Suggests Jeffrey Epstein Was Murdered. His Brother, For One, Feels Validated.

One day in August 2019, Mark Epstein was having breakfast at a Virginia hotel when he looked at the TV and saw CNN reporting that his older brother, Jeffrey Epstein, had died by suicide in a Manhattan federal prison. As jarring as the report was, he had no reason to doubt it.

“I knew he wouldn’t want to live the rest of his life in jail,” Mark told Vanity Fair this week. “He had no children to worry about. Our parents were gone. He knew he didn’t have to worry about me.”

Mark says he finished his omelet and headed back to New York. Then, like so many other Americans, he started to become skeptical of the official narrative.

Over the last seven years, the endless conspiracy theories surrounding Jeffrey Epstein’s death have largely been relegated to the backwaters of YouTube and Reddit, while local and federal authorities have stuck to the suicide story. But this week there was a breakthrough. On Monday, Michael Freeman, a leading forensic scientist who testified for the prosecution in the trial of Derek Chauvin for the murder of George Floyd, issued the most legitimate challenge to date to the prevailing consensus.

Freeman presented his findings at a historic London legal society, saying, “The pattern and distribution and multitude of injuries are not explained by a suicidal hanging.” In a New York Times story published the same day as the presentation, Freeman told the publication that he had no view on who might have killed Jeffrey: “All I’m interested in is, how did this get so sideways?” Along with several global news outlets, including CBS and the BBC, the paper covered the presentation with a straight face even as it noted that Freeman’s efforts to publish his findings in a peer-reviewed journal had thus far been rejected.

The relationship between Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein has loomed large over the president’s second term.

In his thick Brooklyn accent, Mark Epstein, who has long been trying to prove that his brother was murdered while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges, excitedly recounted this new development over the phone the day after Freeman’s presentation, which he attended.

“This crosses all party lines,” Mark said. “Most people believe he didn’t commit suicide. So it’s a mystery. People want an answer to that. I think now they have the answer.”

Mark emphasized that the story of the recent findings was not about him but rather about his brother’s death and Freeman’s work. It was Freeman who reached out to him, Mark said, based on what the scientist independently thought was shoddy work on Jeffrey’s autopsy, and Mark agreed to turn over all the records, reports, and photographs he had as next of kin.

“I want to make it really clear,” he said. “I didn’t pay for this. He’s never asked me for anything other than the information, which I gave him willingly. And he’s been studying this. As a matter of fact, the night before last was the first time I ever met him face-to-face.”

Still, Mark has made his suspicions both his calling card and his personal mission in recent years. After working in real estate investing and serving as the chair of Cooper Union’s board of trustees, he had his own business dealings came under some scrutiny as Jeffrey’s life and crimes dominated political and cultural discourse beginning in the late 2010s—Jeffrey allegedly housed models and employees in an Upper East Side building that was predominantly owned by his brother’s real estate holding company. In the years since his brother’s death, Mark has said that Jeffrey “definitely had dirt” on Donald Trump, and he became a minor fixation amid the Epstein files rollout on account of emails containing banter between him and his brother. (Trump has denied any prior knowledge of Jeffrey’s crimes and said that the release of the Epstein files “totally exonerated” him.) Mark has dismissed a suicide note purportedly written by Jeffrey as a fabrication.

Jeffrey’s death certificate initially said “pending further study” in regard to the cause of death, rather than ruling it a homicide or suicide, but the chief medical examiner ruled it a suicide days later. “All the pathologists I’ve spoken to,” says Mark, “they said, [if] an initial death certificate says ‘pending further study,’ you don’t get an answer usually for weeks or more because something’s being studied.” Mark hired the celebrity forensic pathologist Michael Baden to observe and evaluate the autopsy, and Baden previously stated that “the evidence points to homicide.” Federal officials’ handling of the matter in the years to come only amplified Mark’s concern.

“You know a suicide when you see one,” FBI director Kash Patel said last year while he was under fire for not producing any proof of the Epstein conspiracies he had been touting during his time as a mere conservative podcast personality, “and that’s what that was.”

“I actually laughed out loud when I heard that,” Mark said, “because I thought, How many suicides has this fucking jackass actually seen?”

So who does Mark think killed his brother?

“It’s like in a Mob hit,” he said. “You try to find who the hit man was, and then you try to find who ordered the hit.” The hit man, he figured, could only be someone among a limited number of people: prison employees and other prisoners who had been on Jeffrey’s security tier. “Then the question becomes,” said Mark, “who would have the ability to orchestrate this in a federal prison, and who would have the ability to have the DOJ cover it up?” He couldn’t think of anyone besides Trump. (Trump has not been accused of any wrongdoing in connection to Jeffrey’s death; in a 2023 interview with Tucker Carlson, when asked whether Jeffrey could have been killed, he said, “Oh sure, it’s possible. I mean, I don’t really believe—I think he probably committed suicide.”)

I thought Mark and I had developed some rapport over the conversation, particularly after I mentioned that I’d attended the same Coney Island middle school where he and his brother had been students; I emphasized that I was trying to listen to him carefully and take him seriously. But there was a bit more rancor in his tone after I said it was still difficult to believe that the Department of Justice could have successfully covered up the murder of the most high-profile prisoner in the world.

“If you don’t think that after what I just told you,” Mark said, “then you, sir, are a fucking idiot also.”

#3472. Indie App Spotlight: ‘Milton’ lets you turn your old iPad into a home dashboard

Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

Apple finally released its new HomeView this week, a smart display that serves at the center of your home. What if you don’t want to buy a new product though? Milton is an app for older iPads running iPadOS 17 and later that can serve a similar purpose.

Milton offers a customizable dashboard that allows you to put your most important tiles front and center. It can show your calendar, chores, shopping lists, weather, the clock, a photo frame, a to do list, and so much more. Everything you include will show on the family iPad, but it can also sync to iPhones if you want to check something remotely.

There’s one neat feature that’ll be fun for families: a points system. If your kids complete chores, they can be awarded points and as a parent you can set goals for what kids can earn with enough points. This system can be used to encourage kids to complete chores or follow routines. Parents can also sign off on the chores to ensure kids aren’t just tapping the complete button.

It also serves as a nice recipe guide. If you take photos of cookbooks, Milton can parse through what you captured and provide a step by step guide for cooking. If you don’t have certain ingredients, it can quickly be added to your shoping list.

This only scratches the surface of what Milton can do. You can read their website for the rest.

Here’s why Josh, the developer, decided to build Milton:

I’m a software engineer, and my partner is an oncology pharmacist. She wanted one place that kept our household organised: the calendar, the chores, the shopping, what’s for dinner. Skylight is expensive, and the iPad apps that do this charge a subscription every year. We wanted something that fit our lives, connected us as the Apple family we already are, and didn’t cost families a fortune.

Like most families, we had an old iPad lying around. We put it in a case with a magnet, stuck it to the fridge, and that became Milton.

Milton provides a very generous free offering on the App Store. The core organizer features are all available out of the box, but if you want to add more people to the app, sync across devices, or share the app with other family members (for their personal devices), you’ll need to purchase Milton Individual for $4.99 (one time purchase) or Milton Family for $14.99. Milton Family automatically shares with your iCloud family sharing group.

#3471. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

There are so many A+ celebrity bromances, from Matt Damon and Ben Affleck to Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman. Of course, when talking about such male friendships, Brad Pitt and George Clooney have to be mentioned as well. The two Oscar winners have been friends for years, and a hallmark of the relationship is that the two enjoy taking playful shots at each other. That recently continued during some red carpet interviews, and I’m so glad this trolling between the two prank war participants is still going strong.

Brad Pitt recently stepped out for the Los Angeles premiere of his latest 2026 movie schedule entry, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, where he spoke with ET. During the chat, the news outlet referenced some recent comments that Pitt’s longtime friend and frequent co-star made about his dance moves. Never one to let a joke go unanswered, Pitt humorously clapped back with a take on Clooney’s opinion. Watch Clooney share his initial comments and Pitt drop his rebuttal in the Instagram video below:

A post shared by Entertainment Tonight (@entertainmenttonight)

Spoken like two men who have a friendly rivalry of sorts, and this dynamic goes back quite a while. It was especially present when the pair worked together on the Ocean’s Trilogy, which began back in 2001. Since then, the two have kept their relationship playful, which has led to some great moments. Even earlier this year, Pitt – while promoting his canine-centric movie, Heart of the Beast – mused that a dog could’ve replaced Clooney in Ocean’s Eleven. That’s a great jab but, still, I love Clooney’s take on being able to outdance Pitt:

You know, he’s such a jealous man. In fact, I outdanced him on the dance floor.

Talk about shots fired! Of course, it’s not at all surprising that the F1 star wouldn’t let that humorous critique go unanswered:

I mean, some people live in delusion. What can you say? What are you going to do? You can’t help him.

Of course, the self-deprecating actor also clarified that he couldn’t say with certainty that he’d outdo Clooney. His point was that he doesn’t necessarily “take pride in [his] dancing.” Of course, while Pitt and Clooney may take pleasure in skewering each other from time to time, they do have a genuine friendship and seem to really enjoy being around each other. That playful dynamic was apparently present when they worked on their most recent movie together.

Many may remember that George Clooney and Brad Pitt worked together on 2024’s Wolfs (which is streamable with an Apple TV subscription). Reports indicate that their bromance was alive and well amid production and, while promoting the film, Pitt and Clooney spoke positively of the experience. The jokes were, of course, also flying, and the pair even threw a bit of playful shade at their Ocean’s co-stars during the press tour. And, if all goes accordingly, the pair and their co-stars will be back together again.

Ocean’s Fourteen is in the works, with the surviving cast members reportedly reprising their roles. George Clooney has spoken about the film, and his comments suggest that this won’t just be a legacy sequel cashing in on nostalgia. I look forward to seeing him and Brad Pitt share the screen again, and I also hope that we can look forward to many more years of them trolling each other.

#3469. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to distance myself from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

#3468. Christopher Nolan Reveals Why Watching 'The Odyssey' at Home Is Better than IMAX

The Oscar winning director explains how repeat viewings reveal new layers in his cast's performances and shares his home theater tips.

The Oscar winning director explains how repeat viewings reveal new layers in his cast's performances and shares his home theater tips.

Christopher Nolan has spent much of his career championing the theatrical experience. From shooting on IMAX film to encouraging audiences to see his movies on the biggest screens possible, the director has made no secret of his belief that movies are meant to be experienced in theaters.

But that doesn't mean Nolan thinks watching a movie at home is a lesser experience. In fact, the filmmaker believes home viewing offers some advantages that even the most impressive theater can't replicate. And with The Odyssey arriving on digital, 4K Ultra HD and Blu-ray on Nov. 17, he's encouraging audiences to take advantage of them.

Speaking with Polygon ahead of the film's home release, Nolan discussed how watching a movie in your living room can change the experience, particularly when it comes to appreciating the work of the actors.

"The fun thing about watching a film in the home is a different kind of concentration," Nolan tells Polygon. "When you go to a movie, you're in the dark, you're really focused for a couple hours. In the home, it's a different type of concentration because you can pause the movie, you can go get a snack, come back."

That freedom means viewers engage with a movie differently than they would during a theatrical screening.

"It does allow you to control the timeline and really look at the detail of things," he said. "And for me, it's really about the performances."

While The Odyssey features enormous ships, mythical creatures, and elaborate action sequences, Nolan believes the film's greatest rewards on repeat viewings may come from paying closer attention to its actors.

"The human element is what connects you with the story," Nolan says. "But I think the work of these actors, this cast, this incredible cast in the film, it rewards multiple viewings."

Nolan knows that better than most, having spent countless hours reviewing footage during the editing process. He pointed to the layers in performances by Matt Damon, Anne Hathaway, Tom Holland, Robert Pattinson, and Samantha Morton as details that audiences might appreciate more fully when watching again.

"There's subtleties and nuances in what they're doing that I, in the edit suite, get to watch again and again and again and sort of pick up on all the different things that Matt or Anne or Tom or Rob, what they're bringing to things, or Samantha Morton," Nolan says. "It's really fun for people to be able to look at that in the home and see all the different layers that these guys have put into the story."

When I mentioned that my wife and I enjoy discussing movies while watching them at home, something that isn't exactly encouraged in a theater, Nolan acknowledged the experience has its own appeal.

"It's a different form of engaging with the story, and it has strengths and it has weaknesses," he says. "Nice to be able to sit on your own couch and stretch out, you know what I mean? It's been really exciting over the course of my career to see the leaps forward in terms of technology, in terms of what you're able to do in the home."

Nolan also appreciates how much home-viewing technology has improved during his filmmaking career.

"It's been really exciting over the course of my career to see the leaps forward in terms of technology, in terms of what you're able to do in the home," he says.

And for anyone interested in bringing a little more of the theatrical experience into their living room, Nolan has a suggestion.

"I'm a big fan of projectors," he said. "You can get a relatively low-cost, pretty high-quality projector, darken your living room, maybe introduce some popcorn into the equation or whatever. Have a mini movie theater and do it on your own timeline. That's tremendous fun."

But Nolan doesn't believe a movie necessarily loses its theatrical identity once audiences begin watching it at home. In fact, he suggests that the excitement surrounding a major theatrical release can follow a film into people's living rooms.

"When you have a movie that's played, as The Odyssey has, at length in movie theaters, even viewed in the home, there's a kind of excitement that comes with an event like that," Nolan says. "Even if people are seeing it for the first time, I think the film sort of carries that with it."

The Odyssey arrives on digital, 4K Ultra HD and Blu-ray on Nov. 17

#3467. Beats 360 vs Studio Pro: Here’s which Beats headphones you should buy

In September, Apple introduced the new Beats 360 headphones, the first overears from Beats since the Beats Studio Pro in 2023. That said, the older Beats Studio Pro still remain on sale at a lower price point – so it begs the question, which Beats headphones are more worthwhile?

One of the biggest differences between the two will be the price. The Beats Studio Pro, since they’re older, are regularly available on discount. Currently, you can pick up Beats Studio Pro for $199-249 on Amazon, compared to Beats 360, which aren’t discounted from their $349 launch pricing.

Despite being older and cheaper, the Beats Studio Pro have a couple advantages over the Beats 360. On top of the fact that they’re $100-150 cheaper, you may very well still want to consider them.

The biggest advantages, in my view, have to do with the form factor. The Beats Studio Pro can fold down into a much more compact size, whereas Beats 360 don’t fold at all. This means it’s easier to carry around the Beats Studio Pro.

Beats Studio Pro also offer a headphone jack, whereas Beats 360 don’t have any sort of wired audio at all, even over USB-C. This means Beats Studio Pro are easier to use in environments where bluetooth audio isn’t convenient, such as with a game console or on an airplane.

One of my favorite things about the Beats 360 is that they offer UltraPlush cushions you can swap into, but those cost extra. Beats Studio Pro by default come with UltraPlush cushions, so you can have a more comfortable experience out of the box.

Of course, Beats 360 are newer, so by default they do a number of things better. That includes:

Out of everything on this list, I’d say clearer transparency, stronger noise cancellation, and automatic device switching make the biggest difference. In my testing, its hard to hear with the transparency mode on the Beats Studio Pro, so I end up taking the headphones off to have conversation. With Beats 360, that isn’t the case.

As for noise cancellation and automatic device switching, I feel that if you’re buying Beats for the sake of having Apple headphones, you should buy the ones that offer true automatic device switching – and those are the Beats 360. Noise cancellation is more of a personal preference, but if you value having the best noise cancellation, the Beats 360 are noticeably better.

Lastly, the Beats 360 do have the customizable design going for them. While customization is more aesthetically pleasing, it also has an advantage longer term – when the earcups start wearing down over the years, you can quickly replace them on the Beats 360.

While it’s hard to overlook the fact that Beats Studio Pro come in at a much lower price point, I’d generally say that if you want a great pair of headphones that offer an Apple experience, you probably shouldn’t buy the Beats Studio Pro. The Beats Studio Pro are a fine pair of headphones for the price, but you certainly aren’t getting all of the same ecosystem creature comforts that Beats 360 offer.

That said, Beats 360 simply do not offer a headphone jack or a foldable design, and if those things matter to you, then Beats Studio Pro might still be the way to go. Beats Studio Pro also offer a ton of different color options that aren’t available on Beats 360, while costing $150 less.

#3466. Lux Pascal, Sarah Pidgeon, Ella Rubin, and More Glammed Up for Chanel’s Watches and Fine Jewelry Dinner

“That is the highest compliment you could give anyone!” Lux Pascal says after I tell her she looks like Megan Draper from Mad Men. We’re at Chanel’s Watches and Fine Jewelry holiday dinner, held at Daniel Humm’s new eponymous restaurant, Humm, in the West Village. Pascal is in a ’60s black modish leather minidress that she’s paired with a cat eye. On her wrists are Chanel’s Première Galon watch and Coco Crush bracelets, which, like her rings and earrings, are all dotted with diamonds. As I look around, most of the celebrities dressed by the brand are wearing looks that show off their French fine accessories. Ella Rubin, the Gen Z star of the hit teen TV show Sterling Point, has upgraded a simple pair of vintage Levi’s with a sleek black-and-gold Première Ribbon watch and several diamond rings. This is not a night for hidden gems.

The Pierre Yovanovitch–designed restaurant is a verified New York power room at the moment: There’s Derek Blasberg talking to Sarah Pidgeon about books—War and Peace gets a name-check—and Architectural Digest’s Amy Astley in a corner with Metropolitan Museum of Art board member Robert Denning. Indrė Rockefeller is here, as is stylist Vanessa Traina. In a feat of fun seating arrangements, the Chanel team has sat Rubin next to another young Ella: Beatty, the recent star of Monster and daughter of Warren Beatty and Annette Bening. (Although, with all due respect to those lovely Ellas, the two neighbors I’d most like to eavesdrop on are Devon Lee Carlson and Jack Harlow.) At the bar I hear two fashion people gossiping about industry hiring rumors: “Lauren Sherman says there’s two people in the running,” they whisper about some gig. I think I know what they’re talking about, but not enough to print it.

Laura Love and Devon Lee Carlson on November 17, 2026, in New York City (Photo by Dimitrios Kambouris/WireImage)

Guests mill about because there’s much to mill about: Humm’s filled his restaurant with dozens of notable, site-specific artworks. Louise Bourgeois supplied 24 watercolor paintings, as well as a fantastical sterling silver cast of one of her sculptures, situated by the bar. (Tonight it’s serving mezcal sours with guava and an apple brandy highball.) Francesco Clemente painted not one, not two, but four celestial murals across two months, with motifs of abstract stars, animals, trains, and clocks. On the walls in the main dining room are 12 pigment drawings by Roni Horn. Then there’s all the work by Rashid Johnson: In the lounge—which for this event doubles as a red carpet—hangs his painting Untitled Homes. With Yovanovitch, he also built a custom host stand cast in aluminum and painted red. It’s so textural that you can see the fingerprints, and a number of guests gather around it as the maître d’ explains Johnson’s artistic process like he’s a docent at The Met.

Chanel has decorated the tables with long taper candles and arrangements of deep fuchsia peonies and burgundy garden roses. Waiters serve Humm’s signature everything caviar bagels. When I think about ordering something other than the chicken, a waiter tells me not to. He’s right.

At the end of the night, after most guests are a few glasses of red wine (or martinis) deep, Pidgeon herself grabs a microphone. The event, as it turns out, has a surprise performer: girlsweetvoiced. “She captures something that’s very honest,” Pidgeon says of the emerging singer-songwriter, who then belts out a cover of Joni Mitchell’s “California.” Title aside, it’s been a very New York night.

The hype is real, but what about a movie?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The hype surrounding the long-awaited release of Grand Theft Auto VI has reached a fevered pitch, with reviews for the game universally saying it’s living up to that hype. The GTA series has consistently been one of the most popular gaming franchises of all time, and one of the most successful entertainment franchises on Earth. It’s also one of the only monster franchises that hasn’t been adapted as a movie or a TV show.

That’s always surprised me, because it seems ripe for a video game adaptation, right? Now, the CEO of Take-Two Interactive, the company that owns Rockstar, the studio that produces the games, was recently asked about a possible adaptation. His answer is actually kind of positive news, though hardly concrete evidence that an adaptation is on the way.

While appearing on The David Rubenstein Show, CEO Strauss Zelnick was asked about the possibility of a movie. He responded:

We're very careful about line extensions because this is a creative company, and our goal is to make the best entertainment on Earth.  Entertainment we’re always proud of. We would make a movie or a television show based on our intellectual property if our creative teams were passionate about it, if they thought that would somehow engage and delight our consumers. It's a high bar to do that, and, of course, there's always a risk of failure. So we don't rule it out, but we're very, very selective.

“Line extensions” are when business use existing products or intellectual property to expand how they can take advantage of markets, like, for example, video game movie adaptations. Take-Two, as Zelnick points out, has been very careful with how they’ve expanded their brands outside of video games. No franchise shows that more than GTA. It seems ripe for adaptation and really has been for decades, but they have yet to pull the trigger. They do seem open to it, though.

Like millions of other people, I’m still waiting for a few more hours to be able to play GTA VI, as we all have been for years now. Based on the glowing reviews, this could be the version of the game most likely to get adapted into a movie. Reviews have talked about the storyline in the new game, praising it for how well the story is incorporated into the game. It seems full of drama (and great music). Plus, there are two playable protagonists, a couple named Jason and Lucia.

This is the first time GTA has featured a female playable character, and it tells the story of the two, which to me sounds like the perfect basis for a possible film. While the characters in previous versions have been fun, these two actually sound like the most realistic characters, with a deep backstory together. That really leaves the option open.

It’s also worth mentioning that Zelnick, who took over Take-Two in 2007, has a history in the movie world as the former President of 20th Century Fox and overseeing hit movies like Home Alone and before that worked for Columbia Pictures Television. If anyone knows how to strike a good deal for Take-Two, it’s Zelnick. I would love to see it happen one day!

#3462. Robert Pattinson Is the New James Bond—Revisit 007’s Style Legacy Here

There must be no male character across film history who has done more for menswear—and for the suit—than Bond, James Bond.

That is in part because the sartorial premise of Bond, the suave British spy, is remarkably simple: Presumably, all it takes to embody 007 is a black tuxedo, a sexy watch, and a pair of well-buffed dress shoes. And yet, as Daniel Craig, Pierce Brosnan, Sean Connery, and other dangerously handsome men have proven, a mere suit does not a 007 make. This is why, despite Bond being one of the most popular film characters of all time, you will rarely see ordinary men dare to take him on as a Halloween costume. There’s simply more to making Bond than a good tux.

Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next era of the franchise, now under the creative control of Amazon MGM, and Robert Pattinson has been chosen to reincarnate the character conceived by Ian Fleming in 1953. In the announcement clip for Pattinson’s casting, the actor looks the part in a black tuxedo and white shirt, but it’s his eyes, which pierce through the camera rather than down the barrel of his gun, that do most of the talking and offer a suggestion of what Pattinson’s Bond may have to offer. Will he be a little darker and tortured, like his take on Batman? Or perhaps his Bond will be louche and somewhat pricklier.

A safer bet to make is that he will look good. One of the most enduring legacies of the James Bond franchise is how stylish both the character of Bond and the universe built around him have always been. Bond has appeared classic and timeless in style during each of the franchise’s eras, but hindsight offers a much richer perspective.

Pierce Brosnan, The World Is Not Enough, 1999.

As portrayed through the decades in the property’s famous title sequence, Bond is a silhouette—a classic, timeless silhouette. Fleming established the look in his development of the character when he made the suit his primary uniform. But it is Terence Young, the director of the first 007 films, who is responsible for the visual definition of Bond.

When Connery was cast as Bond for the first film, Dr. No (1962), Young, an avid wearer of suits himself, took him to his own tailor, Anthony Sinclair. We can credit Sinclair with developing the original silver screen Bond look: The suit was lighter in fit and tailoring than most other English suits at the time. The Bond suit had a soft shoulder and waist, but a strong, wide chest and a low button stance that elongated its wearer. Every Bond suit that’s followed has been measured to the standard of Sinclair’s work, and every Bond actor has had to compete with Connery’s charisma while wearing it.

Brosnan and his Brioni suits were indicative of the 1990s corporate look of the time. Craig wore Brioni too, but only for Casino Royale; Tom Ford created his subsequent suiting, which often stood out for the slim fit popular in the 2010s. Most memorable sartorially is Roger Moore’s take through the ’70s and ’80s, which often deviated from the sleekness that had come to define Bond by creating a little frisson with lighter, brighter fabrics and a bolder sense of playfulness.

The character of Bond, and the actor personifying him at a given time, have also become representative of a certain male standard: Connery in the ’60s, tan and athletic, or Brosnan in the ’90s, polished with lithe elegance. And then came Craig, whose casting was met with skepticism, to put it lightly. His arrival was marked by the image of the actor walking out of the ocean in tight swim trunks in Casino Royale. His strong legs, rounded shoulders, and sculpted, hairless chest cemented then and there the idea of what a leading man had become and would look like for the next two decades.

Daniel Craig as James Bond, Casino Royale, 2006.

Also synonymous with Bond are his watch and many vehicles. Most recently, Bond cars have all been made by Aston Martin, though Brosnan drove some spectacular BMWs. The official Bond timepiece since Brosnan’s turn has been Omega. But before such kinds of commercial partnerships were commonplace in Hollywood, Connery wore watches by Rolex, Gruen, and Breitling, while Moore wore pieces by Seiko.

With the news that Pattinson is taking on the mantle, an equally pressing question emerges: Who will be the first new Bond girl?

Some of the most memorable moments in the franchise’s history have been anchored by women. Halle Berry’s emergence from the ocean in an orange bikini and a white belt safekeeping a knife was only made better by the fact that this moment was an homage to the first Bond girl, Ursula Andress, and her ivory two-piece featuring a belt for her own weapon. Then there was Eva Green as Vesper Lynd in a slinky Versace dress in Casino Royale. But it didn’t get better than Grace Jones in A View to a Kill. As May Day, a fabulous femme fatale, Jones wore costumes designed for her by Azzedine Alaïa. How could anyone measure up?

Halle Berry and Pierce Brosnan, Die Another Day, 2002.

Roger Moore and Grace Jones, 1985, A View To a Kill, 1985.

Of course, we will have to see how stylistic choices play out in the 26th Bond film, which, like Bond movies of the past, will become emblematic of the era in which we live. It will also, as a creative project, have to contend with the way Hollywood operates today. The fact that Amazon now has full creative control over the franchise—the company acquired MGM, a co-owner of the Bond franchise rights, for $8.45 billion in 2022 and later struck a deal with the other co-owners in regard to creative authority—is the primary indication of that.

Pattinson will also be the first Bond with airtight fashion-brand deals. Craig was an Omega ambassador as an extension of his role as Bond, which made him a household name, and the 007s who came before him operated within a film industry that was not as closely connected to fashion.

Also unlike his predecessors, Pattinson is stepping into the role as a bona fide movie star who has appeared in three other major franchises (Harry Potter, Twilight, and Batman). He’s already one of the most prolific and bankable stars of his generation, and an undeniable part of being a movie star today is becoming the face of a franchise, a brand, or a product.

In September, Pattinson was announced as a global ambassador for Jaeger-LeCoultre, a Swiss watchmaker. But 007 has worn Omega watches onscreen for decades, a partnership between the brand and the franchise that dates back to the Brosnan years. If Omega’s partnership with the franchise remains for this new installment, it could present a potential conflict if Pattinson’s contract with Jaeger stipulates that he is not allowed to wear another brand’s watch onscreen or front related campaigns for competitors. It may sound like a banal preoccupation, as Pattinson has only just been cast, but there are millions of dollars at play, and actors today often make as much money from brand deals as they do from their turns onscreen.

Pattinson has also been an ambassador for Dior since 2013, serving first as a fragrance ambassador and subsequently as a face for ready-to-wear Dior Homme; he was originally tapped under Kris Van Assche, with his ambassadorship extending through Kim Jones’s tenure at the renamed Dior Men and now continuing with Jonathan Anderson at the helm of the French mega-brand. Will Anderson be providing his suits? The Irish designer has costumed films before, working with Luca Guadagnino on Challengers, Queer, and the upcoming Artificial. To design for the big screen would hardly be a stretch for him.

The real question is more existential: Should Bond wear high fashion? To return to the idea of the 007 silhouette, that in itself is counterintuitive to Pattinson saving the world in one of Anderson’s menswear takes on the famous Dior Bar jacket, with its nipped waist and slightly flared hem. And yet in this brave new world of brand deals, anything is possible.

Obsession is that one film on the 2026 movie schedule that we can’t stop talking about, and why would we want to? Now we can stream it to our heart's content with a Netflix subscription, I needed to dig up all the fun behind-the-scenes facts I learned from writer/director Curry Barker. Each of these made me think of the movie in a whole different way! Let’s get into it. (SPOILERS ahead.)

I’m always curious about how movies change over time, and Barker told CinemaBlend about one pivotal scene that he played around with a lot. The writer/director was also the movie’s editor on the $750k independent production, and he told us about one exchange he tried a bunch of different ways . In his words:

The scene where they’re driving and she’s talking about romance and love. And she’s saying, like, ‘Hey, you know, you’re the only person I can talk to about this stuff.’ That scene changed so much. There’s probably like ten different versions of that scene. One that’s a little longer, one that’s shorter, one where she doesn’t even say the line, one where she goes into a longer thing. Like, I don’t know why. That scene just has so many different versions of it.

This sort of blew my mind because this is the scene I was playing over and over in my head after seeing the movie. It’s an important scene because it establishes Bear and Nikki’s relationship before Nikki loses her autonomy. Watching that scene made me wonder if Bear could have had a shot with Nikki if he had simply asked her out rather than using the One Wish Willow. With that in mind, I totally see why this scene would have needed tweaking, but I think it's perfect now.

When I first watched Obsession, I felt a chill down my spine when Bear called the number on the back of the One Wish Willow box. Then, I subsequently had so many questions about what was going on! When I talked to Barker about this scene, he revealed he was the one on the other side of the line.

Well, that was me… yeah, that’s my voice. He works for the One Wish Willow Company, he kind of answers their phone calls. He handles all the complaints of all the wishes. But, there’s no, I mean, I like to keep it pretty vague. I think you could think of it as some sort of purgatory that [Nikki’s] being kept in, right?

What a fun cameo! I had no idea Barker was the voice, but it’s a fun little tidbit I’ll always think about when I watch that scene. He gave us some interesting insight about what’s going on with that phone call, too. I'm never forgetting Nikki's screams on the other line.

One more BTS detail I want to share has to do with what didn’t make it into the film. Obsession really goes hard in the paint on the movie rating scale, so I was curious if there was a scene the director had to remove because it went too far. The answer is, yes, there was one moment.

There was only one thing I had to take out because it was too far, but other than that they really let me do whatever they wanted. And, I was kind of, like, shocked. This movie really felt like a bunch of kids getting together and making something, and hoping that the parents don’t come home. They never did. Nobody ever stopped us, and we just kept making the thing we wanted to make. Like, even the way we shot it. We thought someone was going to tell us to turn the lights on.

So, what was that “one thing”? During a Q&A (via Deadline), Barker revealed it was the scene where Nikki kills Sarah by smashing her head into the steering wheel. Barker said there was originally “about six or seven more smashes." The MPA ratings board was going to give the movie a NC-17 rating because of it. At first, Barker wasn’t happy about making the change, but when he saw the movie with an audience (and heard their reactions), he realized the number they landed on was “the right number” to choose.

You can check out the rest of our Obsession interview on CinemaBlend's YouTube. There we also talked about that gross cat scene and what probably happens after the ending. I know I’m always finding new theories online. Obsession really is the movie of the year for this horror fan, and I loved learning these behind-the-scenes facts.

#3458. Magic: The Gathering Designer Reveals the Biggest Problem With Marvel’s Infinity Stones

“Three of the six stones are about as blue as it comes.”

When Magic: The Gathering‘s Marvel’s Spider-Man set launched in 2025, the inclusion of The Soul Stone hinted at the scope of Wizards of the Coast’s partnership with Marvel. Including one of the six cosmically powerful gems as the set’s headliner card practically guaranteed the rest would eventually be released, a plan that was confirmed with the printing of The Mind Stone in the 2026 Marvel Super Heroes set. It’s a clever strategy, but one that Magic head game designer Mark Rosewater told Polygon demonstrates a problem with Universes Beyond design.

“We wanted to do something collectible, and we just said to ourselves, ‘In the Marvel property, is there anything that's cool as a collectible?’" Rosewater told Polygon at MagicCon: Atlanta 2026. “Well, the collection of six objects has been the cornerstone of multiple comic book series and the movies. The awareness of the Infinity Stones is so high because of the movies. They are just the obvious choice, so we went with them.”

Rosewater was part of the team that crafted the Infinity Stones as a way to connect the Marvel sets. The cards haven’t been finalized yet, giving Wizards flexibility to fit them into sets as they develop, but the colors and core utility have already been set. They’re all two-cost mana rocks that can be harnessed for a much higher cost to unlock a powerful persistent effect.

“A two-mana stone is just good enough that most decks probably can play that if they want,” Rosewater says. “We make the harnessed ability something that's gated so you don't get it right away, but when you do get it, it can be this pretty glorious thing.”

The hardest part was figuring out how to get six stones to fit into Magic’s five colors.

“One of the challenges of UB is we have to make something attached to our color pie that was not remotely designed for the color pie,” Rosewater says. “Three of the six stones are about as blue as it comes: the Mind Stone, the Space Stone, and the Time Stone. They can’t all be blue. The challenge was to divvy them up. They were close enough to their color matching the color of Magic that we finally decided let’s just make the green stone the green one. If you think of purple and yellow being black and white, we found most of them lined up. There are individual choices that might not be perfect, but each stone is the color that it is was the easiest and simplest way to explain it.”

The Mind Stone became white. The Time Stone will be green and be the headliner for next year's Darkhold Destiny, where its bearer, Doctor Strange, plays a key role in the story. The Space Stone will actually be blue when it appears. Rosewater says his team considered making those three stones blue to go with their thematic affinities, but decided against it.

“It caused a bunch of problems,” he says. “Now blue just has more access than anybody else. That means somebody doesn’t get it, so the people that love that color are yelling at us that everybody gets a two-drop except white. Why doesn’t white get it? For balance purposes and audience expectation purposes, we really, really wanted it to be a cycle.”

The team also considered having a bigger disparity between the core functionality of the cards.

“In the end, we really liked the idea that they’re mana stones,” Rosewater says. “They have a functionality in every deck. If you’re playing that color, you kind of want to play it. The extended effect might not be as effective in your deck, so maybe you don’t play it, but we wanted to make it so a lot of decks of that color would at least heavily consider it.”

There are six Infinity Stones and only five Magic colors. Rosewater says that’s not a problem.

“Magic can do six because we can do five colors and colorless, so Magic has a way to do six that’s built into the game,” he says.

While Wizards of the Coast has stopped short of confirming it outright, that implies we’re due for three more Marvel sets, each prominently featuring the Reality Stone, Power Stone, and Space Stone. The real question is whether Thanos might try to collect them all with the Infinity Gauntlet as some kind of culminating set-based event.

#3457. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

One of the best SNL sketches in years is producing some strong reactions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The goal of sharing a Saturday Night Live sketch is typically to elicit a laugh, but now and again, one makes such a thoughtful or important point that people use it as a conversation starter or as evidence to prove a point. That’s exactly what’s going on with last weekend’s Sister sketch, a fake commercial about how caregiving responsibilities overwhelmingly fall on the women in the family. Tens of thousands have taken to social media to share or retweet the sketch alongside comments about how they feel seen, and now, we’ve reached the point where people are using it to call out their own family members.

Sister has been watched more than five million times in the past few days on YouTube, more than twenty million times on X and untold millions of times more on additional social platforms. If you look at comments on any of these platforms, two immediate themes jump out. Many people are saying they feel exactly like the title sister in the sketch, and many others are calling out family members for not helping with caregiving responsibilities.

Actually, I probably phrased that second one too nicely. What many people are doing is throwing up their middle fingers at family members and telling stories about their avoidance and/ or woeful incompetence. Here’s a story with more than 69,000 likes…

My mom literally called me to come over to help her water a single outdoor plant, and when I got there she was cooking for my older brother who had been there the entire time.

That wild story is definitely not an outlier either. The angry rants are just pouring out of people, an overwhelming majority of whom are women who feel like they are left doing everything while their siblings live their lives. Some are mad about how they did everything until their parent died, only to find out their absentee sibling(s) got the exact same inheritance. Others are mad about how their family members infrequently show up and then critique the job they were doing and question the decisions they make.

One woman shared that a caretaker in her family was later sued by the surviving family members for taking money out of the disabled parent’s bank account to buy said parent food and medicine. You can check out that banger below, which has about five thousand likes…

With Sister you can also wait for her to spend your dad’s money on essentials for him like groceries or clothes and then sue her later - because she never had financial power of attorney!

Seriously, don’t take my word for it. Look wherever the Sister sketch is embedded. You’ll immediately start running into story after story of angry people who need to let it out. I saw one woman calling out the parent they’re looking after for raising her brother to think he didn’t need to help. I’ve seen numerous lawyers, nurses, dementia care workers and doctors saying they see the same dynamic over and over again. I saw one woman say her brother who lives near her mom can’t be bothered to help; so, she has to travel across the country to handle things.

watching this from my mom’s house 1500 miles away bc my brother Just Can’t Manage to get her to the doctor or the dentist. he lives down the street

It’s clear this sketch, which is filled with fun little easter eggs, struck a nerve, but it seems like in a very therapeutic way. It’s allowing people to give voice to frustrations they’ve clearly had for a long time, and if it leads to even some family members doing a little self-reflecting and helping out a bit more, it’ll be a huge victory. You can watch the sketch in full below...

Saturday Night Live is off for a few weeks for the holidays, but it’ll return in early December with the next new episode guest hosted by Amanda Seyfried. Fingers crossed she’s able to give us something that makes even a fraction of the cultural footprint. You can catch previously aired episodes streaming with a Peacock subscription.

#3455. MacBook Neo 2: Here’s everything we know so far

Apple released the all-new MacBook Neo earlier this year, and it’s been a resounding success by all indications. Here’s everything we know so far about what’s next for Apple’s most affordable laptop …

The current MacBook Neo is powered by the A18 Pro chip, which is the same chip used in the iPhone 16 Pro. As reported by Bloomberg, Apple is working on a next-generation MacBook Neo powered by the A19 Pro chip.

In terms of performance, the A19 Pro is about 10-15% faster than the A18 Pro in single-core and multi-core CPU tests. The jump in GPU performance is even bigger, with benchmarks showing an up to 40% boost for the A19 Pro. This is because every GPU core in the A19 Pro has Neural Accelerators built in.

The A19 Pro chip is also used in the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone Air.

According to reporter Tim Culpan, Apple will likely use a “binned” version of the A19 Pro chip in the MacBook Neo. While the A19 Pro chip in the iPhone 17 Pro has a 6-core GPU, the MacBook Neo version of the chip will likely have a 5-core GPU.

One of the compromises of the MacBook Neo is that it has 8GB of RAM. The rest of Apple’s Mac lineup nowadays starts with 16GB of RAM.

The next-generation MacBook Neo won’t jump all the way to 16GB of RAM. Instead, it’s expected to offer 12GB of RAM thanks to the aforementioned A19 Pro.

As I wrote in my review, I don’t think it’s a huge limitation that the MacBook Neo has just 8GB of RAM. Still, an increase for the next-generation model is a great improvement.

The combination of the A19 Pro chip and 12GB of RAM upgrades should also unlock support for Apple’s more powerful on-device AI model announced at WWDC. This model enables a more accurate dictation experience and new options for customizing the Siri voice.

The current MacBook Neo doesn’t support this feature because of its A18 Pro chip and 8GB of RAM.

The MacBook Neo is available in an array of fun colors, including citrus, blush, indigo, and silver. Bloomberg reports that Apple’s plan is to “periodically” update the MacBook Neo with new colors.

There aren’t any details on which colors the next-generation MacBook Neo will be available in.

Apple released the current MacBook Neo in March. Tim Culpan reports that the A19 Pro version of the machine is slated for a release sometime in 2027.

What changes do you want Apple to make with the second-generation MacBook Neo? Are you a MacBook Neo user? Let us know down in the comments.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. Amazon is offering early Black Friday discounts on like-new versions of its 2024 Kindles, with prices starting at $152.99 for the Paperwhite and savings of $27 to $75 across five models that include the color-screen Colorsoft and the pen-equipped Kindle Scribe. All five are a generation behind Amazon's current lineup: The company introduced redesigned Paperwhite and Colorsoft models (plus accessories) in October, with the new Paperwhite now starting at $199.99, and replaced the 2024 Scribe with a third-generation model in December 2025. As for its “like-new” label, it means these are pre-owned devices that Amazon has tested and certified to look and work like new.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite (16GB) is down to $152.99 from $179.99 and covers just about everything most people need for everyday reading, including enough storage for thousands of ebooks. Its seven-inch, 300ppi glare-free display is larger than the previous generation’s 6.8-inch screen, with faster page turns, an adjustable warm light, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. As PCMag notes in its review, it's a great option for readers who don't need color or handwriting features.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $190.99 from $224.99, making it just $38 more than the like-new Paperwhite (16GB). For that relatively small difference, you're doubling the storage to 32GB and getting wireless charging, an ad-free lock screen, and a front light that automatically adjusts to your surroundings—on top of the same sharp seven-inch display, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life as the standard Paperwhite, as noted by this PCMag review.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft (16GB) is down to $220.99 from $260.99 and offers something the Paperwhite models can’t: a color E-Ink display, which makes it well suited to comics, graphic novels, illustrated books, and travel guides. Its seven-inch screen shows that color content at 150ppi while keeping text at a sharp 300ppi, and you can mark passages in multiple highlight colors to keep your notes organized. That said, colors are noticeably more muted than on a conventional tablet, and battery life tops out at eight weeks, compared with 12 weeks on the Paperwhite.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $243.99 from $287.99, making it just $23 more than the standard like-new Colorsoft. For that modest increase, you're getting twice the storage at 32GB, which is particularly useful for comics, manga, and graphic novels that take up more space than regular ebooks, along with wireless charging, an automatically adjusting front light, and an ad-free lock screen. However, as PCMag notes in its review, the color display produces more subdued tones than a conventional tablet, so the Paperwhite remains the more economical choice if you primarily read novels.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $284.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. Unlike the other Kindles here, it's built for reading and writing, with a 10.2-inch, 300ppi glare-free display and a Premium Pen with an eraser and shortcut button—making it the most versatile option for readers who want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

After considerable speculation and a plethora of reports, it was finally confirmed this week that Robert Pattinson would take on the mantle of James Bond. I personally didn’t have my money on the Batman actor trading in his cape for a suit, but I'm not mad at it! Now, additional details are starting to reach the surface, as it's been alleged that Pattinson was pulled into an audition after executives were struggling to make a decision. With that, he was allegedly paid a large sum of money to test for the role, and it seems a lot more of that green could come his way.

According to a report from The Mirror, the Dune actor received $1 million just to audition for 007. To say that's a considerable amount of money would be an understatement. However, Amazon MGM Studios has neither confirmed nor denied that total. As surreal as that sum might seem, there's more to this.

Pattinson -- who has since been congratulated by the British Royal Family and more -- the Royal Family welcomed him as the next Bond. Apparently, the Drama star has signed a three-year deal to play Commander Bond and could allegedly make somewhere between £58 million ($76 million) and £75 million ($98 million). Again, none of this is confirmed, but such a paycheck would make sense, given the deal and the sheer size of this storied IP.

Meanwhile, fans have mixed reactions to the casting news, with some already on board with seeing Pattinson’s take on 007 and others feeling like there were other prime options. A number of notable stars were in the mix before Pattinson was cast, with Jack Lowden notably emerging as a reported favorite. Some may wonder how Pattinson was decided upon and, per an insider, the process wasn't cut and dry.

Per a source for The Mirror, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' wife, Lauren Sanchez, was a major proponent of Robert Pattinson being cast in the role. Sanchez has allegedly long been a fan of the Primetime star and supposedly helped push him to the forefront when it came to Bond casting. The insider said:

Robert wasn’t the name everyone was talking about. There were other actors who seemed much further down the road. Then, suddenly, he was the man everybody wanted. Lauren’s push for him was hardly a secret in certain circles. Jeff might be the man with the billions, but Lauren has his ear.

Details on Bond 26 are being kept under wraps, including the title and premise. At this point, it also feels unlikely that it'll be released in 2027. However, we do know that Denis Villeneuve will be directing the movie, meaning this will be a Dune reunion for him and Pattinson. There is a lot of speculation surrounding who will join Pattinson, as names are being thrown out for the next Bond villain. And, of course, many are wondering who will be the next Bond girl with rumors placing Margaret Qualley in the lead as a strong candidate.

Regardless of what actually unfolds within the next 007 movie, this new report suggests that Robert Pattinson will be well compensated for the role. What's more is that this reported deal comes near the end of a year that saw him headline multiple high-profile movies. And, of course, can be seen in the upcoming Dune: Part Three, as well as 2028's The Batman: Part II. Needless to say, the man is booked and busy.

Pattinson's clearly come a long way, from playing a sparkling vampire in Twilight to playing a doomed young wizard in Harry Potter. Now, he can add being the ninth James Bond to his resume (and his bank account may be fuller for it).

#3452. How To Watch The Social Reckoning At Home

"The Social Reckoning" is finally hitting the home market. It will become available to buy or rent on digital starting November 24, 2026, prior to its physical media release on January 12, 2027.

In case you're unfamiliar with "The Social Reckoning" writ large, here's the gist. Almost two decades after he won an Academy Award for writing the screenplay for "The Social Network," a 2010 dramatization of the founding of Facebook directed by David Fincher, Aaron Sorkin decided to make a sequel that focuses on what Facebook has become in the 2020s. Jesse Eisenberg, who earned an Oscar nod for playing Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg in "The Social Network," declined to return to the role and was replaced by "Succession" veteran, Emmy and Tony winner, and Sorkin's "The Trial of the Chicago 7" collaborator Jeremy Strong. With Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White, Bill Burr, Wunmi Mosaku, Betty Gilpin, and Billy Magnussen starring alongside Strong, the project seemed almost too big to fail before it premiered in theaters on October 9, 2026.

Fail it did, though. Though it reportedly only lost a couple million for Sony (per Deadline), the film absolutely underperformed at the box office, and its rating on Rotten Tomatoes is a middling-to-bleak 54%. So what happened here? Well, from my perspective, "The Social Reckoning" is just a bad movie ... and /Film's chief film critic Chris Evangelista agrees with me. What went wrong as Sorkin tried to make a legacy sequel to one of the best films of the 21st century? Quite a lot actually!

I'll circle back to the "Social Network" of it all shortly, but the bottom line here is that "The Social Reckoning" just ... stinks to high heaven. From the embarrassing prologue featuring Portia Doubleday as a caricature named Kayleigh (I'm not kidding) to the fact that Aaron Sorkin keeps forcing Oscar winner Mikey Madison into outfits that would make her title character from "Anora" blush (in the name of corporate espionage), I found "The Social Network" to be a uniformly dreadful watch from start to finish. Not only is the script clunky as all hell — unfortunately, an ongoing problem with many of Sorkin's recent screenplays — but the story is attempting to make some sort of larger point that doesn't just fall flat but thuds directly to the floor. We already know social media makes everyone angry and insane, and we also know that social media has contributed to right-wing radicalization. Sorkin making a movie that beats us over the head with these two ideas and also ends in a full recreation of the January 6, 2021 insurrection is just as bad as it sounds in theory.

It's also incredible to me that Sorkin managed to cast a lot of great actors and coach them into giving some of the worst performances of their careers. Madison is an enigmatic and compelling performer, and Sorkin transforms her into the robotic Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen, a deeply unlikable person who doesn't seem to understand human behavior. Jeremy Allen White's journalist Jeff Horwitz is nothing but an exposition machine, and Jeremy Strong's Mark Zuckerberg has no interiority and sounds like Kermit the Frog. The only person who's good in this movie is Bill Burr. Think about that for a second.

"The Social Network" might be one of my very favorite movies of all time, but I can tell you, from a completely unbiased perspective, that "The Social Reckoning" is a wholly undeserving sequel to that 2010 masterpiece. It's clear now, with plenty of hindsight and movies like this, that "The Social Network" was good because of director David Fincher and despite Sorkin. To be fair to Sorkin, he basically admitted that to The Hollywood Reporter after "The Social Reckoning" got soundly panned.

"I would have rather David Fincher directed it — I would rather David Fincher direct everything — but David has an exclusive deal at Netflix, and this was owned by Sony," Sorkin told the outlet on their "Awards Chatter" podcast. Not only did Sorkin also admit that he's "very worried that the parts of directing that [he's] not good at are those parts that you can't learn," he also said, "I was surprised by how little of the science of filmmaking I'd managed to absorb [from other directors] ... I have no visual sensibility, it turns out."

I have to agree with him. Despite the same cinematographer — Jeff Cronenweth — working on both "Network" and "Reckoning," the sequel is visually bland, unimaginatively shot, and even recycles a couple reaction and establishing shots throughout its run time. Basically, "The Social Reckoning" is a poorly made film that I cannot in good conscience recommend; in fact, I'd recommend you just watch "The Social Network" instead. But if you're still interested, you can check out "The Social Reckoning" at home once it's available.

#3451. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.
