#3377. 10 Hacks Every Hulu User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you don't like the content Hulu is suggesting for you, you have several options to curate your recommendations. "Disliking" a show or movie removes it from your Home view and You May Also Like entirely, so the only way you'll see that content is if you search for it. You can dislike on the Details page if you're watching on your TV or use the thumbs down on mobile or web. (The "Like" button will obviously influence your algorithm in the opposite way). If your "Continue Watching" queue is cluttered with shows you started but didn't like enough to finish, you can remove them from your watch history as well as the My Stuff list. This, too, will allow content to remain searchable but not suggested in other areas of the app.

If PIN protection is enabled, users must enter a four-digit PIN when switching between profiles on a single account. This is intended as a parental control feature, since it's available on non-Kids profiles and can keep children from accessing more mature content on an adult's profile. However, you can also enable this feature to keep other users from seeing your viewing history and preferences or influencing your algorithm by watching their content under your profile (accidentally or on purpose). To set up a PIN, log into your account on Hulu's website, select your profile, and go to Manage Profiles > Parental Controls. You'll have to choose a PIN and enter your password to confirm the changes.

Another approach to protecting your profile and algorithm is to set up separate profiles for specific use cases, such as when you have guests or if you host watch parties for certain shows. This keeps content from influencing your recommendations and prevents other viewers from seeing what's in your watch history or saved content (especially if there are things you want to keep private).

If you find that subtitles and captions are too bold—or not visible enough—you can change the font, color, size, and style from the default so they enhance your viewing experience rather than detracting from it. Hulu allows you to adjust the color and opacity of the font, background, and window so you get the right contrast, and you can also select the specific font and font scaling. On your streaming device, go to Settings > Subtitles & Captions, then hit the back button on your remote to save your preferences. You can update these settings on mobile and desktop as well.

If you have a long list of shows and films to watch but can't decide what to start next, look for the "Expiring Soon" badge to see which titles are leaving the service in the next two weeks. Badges display the number of days remaining, so you can determine what to prioritize and whether it's worth diving in based on how much time you have to finish before the expiration date. Go to "My Stuff" to monitor saved titles that are expiring soon.

If you've been watching Hulu under an account shared with family or friends and need to switch to your own subscription, you can transfer your profile to keep your watch history and settings intact instead of starting from scratch. You can initiate a profile transfer on a TV-connected device. Note that account holders have to approve transfer requests within seven days, and once expired, transfer requests cannot be resubmitted—so be sure to let the primary user know that you've made the request.

If you've shared your Hulu login information with friends or activated your account on devices you don't own, you may want to regularly audit where your account is being used and remove any that don't need access. This includes TVs in Airbnbs and hotels. If you stay logged in, unauthorized users may have access to your Hulu account and personal data. You can see activated devices (and their activation date) under Your Account > Watch Hulu on Your Devices > Manage Devices. Click Remove next to old or unrecognized devices.

Hulu has an offline mode that allows you to download shows and movies to watch when you don't have a network connection. This is useful for traveling or when you know your wifi or cell service will be limited. Downloads are only available on supported iOS and Android devices, which means you may have to consider how much space your content takes up. You can select High for video quality if you want maximum resolution, but you may want to choose Standard if you are short on storage. This option is available under Downloads > Settings > Video Quality on iOS and Account > Settings > Downloads > Video Quality on Android. Note that once you click play on downloaded content, you have 48 hours to watch it before it expires—so don't start it unless you are ready.

If you have a Hulu + Live TV subscription, you must designate a "Home" network, which determines the local channels included in your plan. You can update your location up to four times within a 12-month period, but this limitation is meant to prevent viewers outside a household from sharing a subscription. Hulu does allow you to stream live TV on mobile when you're away from your home network (within the U.S.) as long as you access your account on that network every 30 days. If you travel often, check in with your mobile device frequently to avoid being locked out when you're away. Note that you can still watch streaming content with no restrictions.

#3375. How to Make Sure an 'Onion' Site on the Dark Web Is Legitimate

Thankfully, Tor Browser already has a cryptography-backed feature that can verify the authenticity of an onion site, by confirming whether it has end-to-end encryption and extended validation certificates. Here's how this feature works, where it falters, as well as what other red flags you should look for.

While phishing on the dark web works as it does on the clear web, scammers have a few unique advantages due to the secretive nature of the environment. Most importantly, you can’t just glance at an onion link to tell if the site is genuine. Normal website URLs tend to be short and memorable, while onion links are 56-character strings of alphanumeric text that look mostly like gibberish.

When you try to connect, Tor Browser verifies the URL against the originating website’s cryptographic key, which is how you know nobody has hijacked the address or tampered with it midway. But since this has the unwanted effect of making domains harder to recall, scammers have a much easier time generating lookalike addresses or creating website clones.

For example, many popular websites use “vanity prefixes” to make their onion addresses more easily identifiable or to add some branding appeal. That means their 56-character onion link starts with something like “facebook,” “bbcnews,” or “ciadotgov.” But scammers can use a free tool like mkp224o to generate lookalike addresses with the same vanity prefix as the legitimate website, which gives users a false sense of security.

Of course, most dark web users don’t type addresses directly into Tor Browser; they use dark web directories like the Hidden Wiki to find useful onion sites relevant to their search. Scammers will create fake search engines or link directories to point users to their fake websites, like when the Ahmia search engine discovered that a copy of its platform was directing users to 255 cloned services back in 2015.

Of course, it’s possible to orchestrate phishing attempts that don’t involve cloning sites at all. Researchers at Freie Universität Berlin describe a sophisticated technique where attackers serve the real website through their own reverse proxy, which lets them manipulate parts of the site or log your online activity without your awareness. In 2019, ESET even found a trojanized version of Tor Browser that replaced Bitcoin addresses on websites to direct payments to hackers. So both genuine websites and your browser itself are also vulnerable to manipulation if you download or access them from an unverified source.

There are a few best practices to avoid phishing attacks when using the dark web. None of them are foolproof on their own, but together, they considerably lower the risk of ending up on a fake or manipulated website.

On the desktop version of Tor Browser, you can access an onion site using a shortened version of its URL called an Onion Name. For now, this feature only works with SecureDrop, so newsrooms can establish tip lines with addresses like mysitename.securedrop.tor.onion, which would then redirect to the 56-character original onion address. This feature is in active development, so more platforms might support it in the future.

When you load up an onion site using the Tor Browser, you’ll see an onion icon on the address bar, which confirms that your connection is end-to-end encrypted. But you can also click on the onion icon to check if the site has an Extended Validation (EV) certificate, which tells you that its authenticity has been verified by a trusted certificate authority like DigiCert. While not every legitimate onion site will have an EV certificate, famous ones like Facebook tend to.

On the other hand, if you see a caution sign next to the onion icon, that means the site is using a self-signed or expired certificate that isn’t guaranteed by a trusted authority. It may also imply that the site is being served over an insecure URL. This doesn’t definitely tell you it’s a phishing site, but it’s a red flag to watch out for nevertheless.

Don’t rely on search engines, link directories, Reddit threads, or Telegram channels too heavily on the dark web. Once you’re sure you’ve found the onion address for a genuine site, bookmark it so you can access it directly the next time you want to visit.

If you realized that you’ve been the victim of a phishing attempt, the first step is to close the browser window with the fake site and access the real onion address to reset any account passwords you may have accidentally divulged.

Also, generally try to enable two-factor authentication and PGP logins on any dark web account that supports it for added security. And if you downloaded Tor Browser from anywhere other than the official Tor Project site, uninstall it now and grab a fresh copy from the official address.

#3372. Clint Eastwood Nearly Directed A Star Is Born With Beyoncé

Bradley Cooper and Lady Gaga's chemistry helped make 2018's A Star Is Born a success, but its musical performances were just as important. Cooper made his directorial debut playing Jackson Maine, a country-rock musician dealing with alcoholism. Gaga played Ally, an undiscovered singer who catches Jackson's attention at a drag bar. Their romance develops alongside Ally's rising career, creating tension as Jackson's struggles worsen. Their performance of "Shallow" marks a turning point, as Jackson brings Ally onstage to perform her original song, introducing her talent to a much larger audience and helping launch her career.

However, the version audiences eventually saw was far from the only one being considered. Years before Cooper stepped behind the camera, Clint Eastwood was attached to direct his own remake of A Star Is Born, with Beyoncé set to play the leading lady (via Los Angeles Times). The pairing was an interesting one, especially given Eastwood's longstanding interest in jazz and Beyoncé's career as one of the biggest names in contemporary music (via Shadow and Act). It was also a serious project backed by Warner Bros.

Eastwood's remake never made it into production, and the project underwent several changes before Cooper brought his interpretation to theaters (via BAFTA). Although Eastwood's version would have followed the same basic story, his approach to the music and Beyoncé's involvement could have given the film a different identity. Each major version of A Star Is Born has reflected the entertainment industry of its time, and Eastwood had specific ideas about the music he wanted to explore. His plans for Beyoncé and the circumstances that eventually brought Cooper aboard reveal how differently the 2018 remake could have turned out.

When Eastwood signed on to direct A Star Is Born in 2011, Beyoncé had already been attached to the project for several years. According to TheWrap, the remake had gone through several potential directors before Eastwood became involved. Screenwriter Will Fetters had developed a version focused on a rising female singer and an older, fading performer, although the production had yet to secure its male lead.

Eastwood also had specific ideas about the film's music. In a 2012 interview reported by Shadow and Act, he discussed Beyoncé's interest in writing songs for the movie and his desire to introduce her to jazz. He even compared her vocal abilities to those of Sarah Vaughan and Ella Fitzgerald, suggesting a musical direction quite different from Cooper's eventual adaptation.

In Cooper's film, Jackson's country-rock sound contrasts with Ally's transition toward mainstream pop, capturing the growing distance between their careers. Eastwood's interest in jazz could have given the characters a different sound, especially if Beyoncé contributed original songs. Although the full soundtrack was never produced, his comments suggest he wanted to explore a different side of her talents.

Clint Eastwood's A Star Is Born faced several setbacks before Beyoncé officially departed in October 2012. Production was initially reportedly delayed by her pregnancy, while scheduling conflicts and difficulties securing a male lead complicated the project further. According to the Los Angeles Times, several actors were considered for the role, including Tom Cruise, Leonardo DiCaprio, and Bradley Cooper. However, the musical movie never moved forward with Eastwood directing.

Cooper had actually been approached by Eastwood about starring in the remake, but initially felt he was too young for the role. After working together on 2014's American Sniper, Cooper eventually became interested in developing his own version of A Star Is Born. Interestingly, Beyoncé remained part of his plans for a time. During a BAFTA career retrospective, Cooper explained that he had written his adaptation with her in mind before considering Adele.

Ultimately, Cooper found his leading lady after watching Lady Gaga perform "La Vie en Rose" at a cancer fundraiser. Impressed by Gaga's performance, Cooper approached her about playing Ally, and the two began developing the film together. Their collaboration ultimately brought A Star Is Born to theaters in 2018, with a different director, leading actress, and musical direction than Eastwood had originally envisioned.

#3370. Scott Speedman Officially Leaves ‘R.J. Decker’ Behind for Taylor Sheridan’s ‘Landman’ Season 3

Taylor Sheridan has had a lot going on this year, but that isn’t all that surprising to those who have been following his work since the early days of Yellowstone. There are also those who have been around for his projects since before he ever wrote an episode of Yellowstone — back in 2015, Sheridan made his feature writing debut on Sicario, the neo-Western crime thriller starring Josh Brolin and Emily Blunt. After writing the 2018 Sicario sequel, Day of the Soldado, Sheridan is not involved with the third Sicario movie that was confirmed a few weeks ago. Steven Knight, writer of Peaky Blinders and the new Robert Pattinson-led James Bond movie in the works at Amazon, is writing the script for the film with Padraic McKinley (The Weight) set to step behind the camera and direct.

The most exciting project on the horizon for Sheridan is, without a doubt, the third season of Landman. It was thought that Landman Season 3 would make it back to Paramount Plus before the end of the year, but several production delays led to the show being pushed back to 2027. However, cameras on Landman Season 3 are rolling, with new cast members such as Michael Kelly (Lioness) being announced on almost a weekly basis. This afternoon, the cast of the show grew even further, when news broke this afternoon that Scott Speedman, best known for starring in R.J. Decker and Running Point, has officially joined the cast of Taylor Sheridan's Landman Season 3. Details about his role are being kept under wraps for now. No word yet on if his guest starring role will be limited to one episode or if he will be a recurring guest star.

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

Heading into Landman Season 3, most major cast members such as Ali Larter, Demi Moore, and even Michelle Randolph are receiving huge pay bumps for their roles in the third season. The only cast member returning and not receiving a raise is Billy Bob Thornton, who stars in the leading role as Tommy Norris. Thornton isn’t eligible for a raise yet because he originally inked a three-season deal to star in the show. Should it be renewed for Season 4, he’s in line for a massive payday.

Check out the first two seasons of Taylor Sheridan’s Landman on Paramount Plus and stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of the series.

#3368. ‘Artificial’ Trailer: Andrew Garfield Stuns in Luca Guadagnino’s Sharp, Shocking, Funny Portrayal of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman

Luca Guadagnino takes on — and potentially takes down — artificial intelligence and one of its figureheads with his latest feature film, “Artificial.”

A swishy, swively, veering-toward-camp Andrew Garfield plays gay OpenAI CEO Sam Altman opposite an ensemble that includes Oscar-nominated “Anora” breakout Yura Borisov as his former chief scientific officer Ilya Sutskever, Monica Barbaro as erstwhile OpenAI chief technology officer Mira Murati, Ike Barinholtz as an outré Elon Musk, along with Cooper Hoffman, Mark Rylance, Jason Schwartzman, Chris O’Dowd, and Zosia Mamet.

Ahead of the film’s release from Neon on Christmas Day, watch the trailer below. Related Stories ‘The Comeback King’ Trailer: Glen Powell Is a Cancelled Country Star in Judd Apatow’s Latest Directing Project ‘Gentle Monster’ Review: Léa Seydoux Learns the Truth About Her Husband in Marie Kreutzer’s Tough Study of Child Sex Abuse

Written by former “Saturday Night Live” scribe Simon Rich, “Artificial” dramatizes a two-decade artificial intelligence arms race. AI-pioneering professor Geoffrey Hinton makes a vanguard discovery that will change the course of humanity forever — with Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and more prominent Silicon Valley techbros racing to get in on the vision, inevitably leading to corruption that Guadagnino details with scary prescience. Especially as Ilya falls deeper and deeper under Sam Altman’s frighteningly charismatic sway.

As IndieWire’s David Ehrlich previously wrote, “Guadagnino is exploring how difficult it is to abandon the body in the first place — and not just the body, but the intangible essence that it contains. We couldn’t leave it behind if we tried, and this, in his own way, is Guadagnino trying just as hard to do that as Sam Altman ever did.”

“Artificial” was something of an industry hot potato for a sizable stint over the summer, with Amazon MGM Studios dropping the film (which it produced) allegedly over its own ties to artificial intelligence and Altman. Neon eventually picked up “Artificial,” marking the indie company’s first partnership with the “Call Me by Your Name” and “Challengers” director, whose last movie was “After the Hunt,” also at Amazon MGM Studios. “Artificial” surprise-premiered at the New York Film Festival to strong praise — the same week that Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Network” sorta-sequel “The Social Reckoning” failed to generate much noise.

Neon will take the film into wide release over the Christmas holiday. It’s indeed one of the most crowd-pleasing (and also darkest) films of Guadagnino’s career. (Earlier in December, IndieWire Honors will celebrate the film’s cast at our December 3 event.)

The cover - by Nick Dragotta and Frank Martin - was shared on social media, with the caption "Who says the Absolute Universe can't be cute?" The image shows a baby playing with Batman's cowl and cape while Bruce and Selina stand reflected in Catwoman's mirrored helmet.

Behind the baby is a repeated 'HAHA' motif suggesting the Joker/Jack Grimm's involvement, with the arc title 'THE DEMON CHILD' appearing alongside.

In Absolute canon, Bruce and Selina are childhood friends who grew up together, with a young Bruce Wayne working for gang lord Falcone at one point due to his threats on Selina's life. As adults, Bruce became a vigilante and Selina became a professional thief. The two recently met up, apparently conceiving a child during the period when Batman was fighting Bane.

Underneath DC Comic's Instagram post, fans have been debating the identity of the child. While some think it's Damian Wayne (Bruce's mainstream son with Talia al Ghul) others argue it's Helena Wayne, Bruce's alt-universe daughter with Catwoman, who grows up to become the vigilante Huntress.

The title 'The Demon Child' suggests it's Damian, with the 'al Ghul' family name literally meaning 'the demon.' However, Snyder previously said he wouldn't be adapting Damian, and the Absolute Universe - especially Absolute Batman - is built on wrongfooting fans. This is a world where Bruce is close friends with the Penguin and Two-Face and is hunted through the streets by his various Robins, so anything is possible.

The laughter on the cover image is a good reason for fans to be fearful. In this world, Joker is an immortal billionaire who carries out wide-ranging superhuman experiments, creating monsters including Mr. Freeze, Poison Ivy, Man-Bat and more. There are a LOT of ways Joker could be messing with Bruce. For instance, Absolute Clayface is a shapeshifter who has copied his genetic code - this may not even be Selina.

It's also worth noting that Absolute Scarecrow's introduction introduced a byzantine maze of bluffs and plans manipulating both Bruce and his family, including faking the survival of his father Thomas Wayne. Scarecrow would and could fake a Wayne baby, and while Selina doesn't have any direct ties to Joker, she's a professional criminal in a world where he wields immense influence.

Fans will find out the truth as Absolute Batman's 'The Demon Child' unfolds, but given everything Bruce has been through in the series so far, it's likely to be a bumpy, twisted ride.

Absolute Batman #25 is available now from DC Comics.

#3362. 10 Shows Like 'The Traitors' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What started as De Verraders way back in 2021 has become a global reality phenomenon: Peacock in the U.S. hosts the American version with the sartorially supreme Alan Cumming, and also the earlier UK take as well as iterations from Australia, Canada, and New Zealand—but there are spin-offs in France, India, Germany, Ireland, Turkey, and more. Basically, throw a dart at a map and you're likely to hit a country with its own take on The Traitors. And yet! The addictive nature of reality TV means that we can't really ever get enough. In that spirit, here's more backbiting reality TV, and a couple of dramas that offer up similarly duplicitous thrills.

A reality show with a complex history as relates to The Traitors, the premise being so similar that it may well have served as an inspiration. Here, players participate in collaborative missions in order to build a prize fund. But it's not all fun and games: There's a secret double agent among the group (the mole, obviously) whose sole task is to undermine the ability of the rest of the group to earn money. Eliminations are done via quiz: The group is grilled on the information they've collected about the mole, and whoever knows the least gets the boot. Originally airing in the aughts, Netflix brought it back for a couple of seasons more recently, with the potential for more to come. Stream the most recent seasons of The Mole on Netflix.

If there were a prize for dramatic title (and set design), you could do a lot worse than this one. In this South Korean reality show, 12 celebrity contestants are challenged to build a prize pot through strategy games. Sometimes they're collaborative, sometimes entirely competitive, and sometimes a blend, but prizes come in the form of "Pieces" that can be won or lost (and that eventually combine to create their own final puzzle). Anyone who finds themselves without a single Piece is out. Pieces can be spent to buy advantages, and also traded, so the show turns on players forming alliances in order to build the prize pot and survive as long as possible. Stream The Devil's Plan on Netflix.

Here, a bunch of strangers are holed up in an apartment building, cut off from the outside world—and each other. Players can only interact via a custom app, and, thus, can portray themselves however they want, whether that means being 100% genuine (unlikely!) or creating a whole new persona. Players judge the competition based on their interactions, determining the "Influencers" who will get to decide on the eliminations. The show ran for seven seasons on Netflix, and is moving to Hulu for the forthcoming eighth. Stream The Circle on Hulu.

You show up at a fancy hotel, and someone hands you a suitcase containing one million dollars. It's yours to keep—as long as you can keep it a secret. In this one, all the contestants get a suitcase, and only one contains the money. Much as with The Traitors, the goal is to figure out who's keeping the secret, with challenges designed to help flush that person out. If the truth is discovered via a vote, that former millionaire is ousted and the money is concealed in another suitcase until the final contestants are given the opportunity to swap bags with someone who they think has the money. Easy come, easy go, I guess. Stream Million Dollar Secret on Netflix.

I'm a little more into the normies on Traitors myself, but there's no question that a big part of the appeal (for most seasons) is watching reality-show celebs go at it with cash on the line. So it is with House of Villains, a Big Brother-style competition with Joel McHale as ringmaster. The core premise is pretty simple: villains (Richard Hatch, Tom Sandoval, Jonny Fairplay, one-time Trump bestie Omarosa Newman, etc.) compete in challenges for rewards and for safety from the inevitable banishment. It's all mostly an excuse to watch some of TV's biggest personalities go for each other's jugulars. Stream House of Villains on Peacock.

This is not a reality show, but rather a drama about a reality show that may well slake your thirst for treachery while offering up consequences a bit more dramatic than the bruised egos and hurt feelings of The Traitors. Here, eight strangers are selected to compete in a game in which they're locked together in a building and sequestered on different floors each night. They earn money for each minute they last in the game, but all their provisions must be purchased with money they've won, at an extreme markup. At first, the contestants pool their resources so that everyone gets more money—until they learn that people on higher floors are getting more. Then things get nasty Stream The 8 Show on Netflix.

This one plays a bit like The Traitors in reverse: A $250,000 prize pot is, right off the bat, allocated to all 11 contestants who get to hang out in a luxurious villa. So the game isn't about winning money so much as it is about how much you'll keep and how much you're willing to share. Eliminations offer the opportunity to remove those who the others don't want to share with—though contestants don't have to actually ever vote anyone out. They can just keep their portion of the money and hang out, something that obviously does not happen. Challenges along the way force contestants to reveal embarrassing and sometimes ugly truths about themselves that may well put them on the outs with the others. There's only one season at present, though there's potential for more. Stream The Trust on Netflix.

Blending the Big Brother-esque social aspects of Traitors with Survivor's love of the great outdoors, this one drops four teams of four into the Alaskan wilderness (moving to Panama for season three). The contestants are all, by inclination, loners, but the game has only one core rule: Only a team (of at least two) can win, so while the game has the typical reality show eliminations, these wilderness enthusiasts must work together in order to take the money. In the same way that The Traitors creates a tension between competition and cooperation via its communal prize pot, Outlast sees its contestants forced to maintain relationships whether they like it or not. Stream Outlast on Netflix.

The tasks on Traitors aren't typically the most thrilling part of the show, which makes this James Bond-branded competition a solid match if you want more complicated and better developed challenges. In this one, nine teams of two visit exotic locations in each episode and compete in spy-themed activities with the ultimate goal of winning £1 million by making it to the end. It leaves out the bits where people sit around a castle strategizing, but it includes, like Traitors, a dapper Scotsman not afraid to camp it up—in this case, Brian Cox, serving as the spymaster who directs the teams in their missions. Stream 007: Road to a Million on Prime Video.

Squid Game: The Challenge would probably be a more reasonable choice for this list—given that it's a proper reality show and not a blood-chilling thriller. But I'm sticking with the original drama here since, as perfectly entertaining as that spin-off is, it feels like it misses the point. In the original (surprise smash hit) drama, 454 needy contestants are recruited for a new reality competition in which they're tasked to play rather simple children's games—with deadly consequences that are cheered on by the wealthy financiers who are willing to pay good money to watch both the poors go at each other, as people turn on each other to survive and to win the rather shockingly large prize. A bit like The Traitors if all of Alan's murder schtick were literally true. Stream Squid Game on Netflix.

#3361. Apple reveals how iCloud+ increases Siri AI and Apple Intelligence usage limits

iOS 27.3 beta 2 is now available, and Apple is adding the ability for users to unlock higher usage limits for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI via iCloud+. Here’s everything you need to know.

From the start, Apple has said that some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features have usage limits because “they rely on powerful server models.” The company previously outlined that increased access would be available across most iCloud+ subscription plans, and now we have the full details on how this will work.

Apple says the new system applies to several categories of Apple Intelligence features, including:

The usage limits are per device, not per account. This means your iPhone, iPad, and Mac each have separate allowances. Apple isn’t disclosing specific limit numbers. Instead, it says that limits can vary based on the feature, request complexity, system demand, and more.

As you near your limit, you’ll see an alert within whichever feature you’re using. For example, if you are using Image Playground, a message will appear telling you that you’ve almost hit your usage limit for the day. Once you hit the limit, you’ll be prompted to wait for it to reset or upgrade your iCloud+ plan.

If you hit your limit, basic Siri requests will still work. This includes things like setting timers and alarms. Requests that require Siri to understand personal context and perform more complex, multi-step actions, however, are subject to the limits.

For example, asking Siri to find the details of an upcoming dinner reservation in your email and add them to your calendar would count toward your daily limit.

Additionally, each device uses its own standard daily usage limit first. After that, it can tap into the additional capacity included with an eligible iCloud+ subscription:

The usage unlocked by iCloud+ is shared across all devices signed in to your Apple Account, as well as family members sharing your iCloud+ plan. The shared usage is available on a first-come, first-served basis

All limits will reset daily at the same time, and limits don’t roll over. In most cases, limits reset around midnight in your current time zone.

Apple has published a support document with more details.

#3360. One of the Best Comic Anti-Heroes of All Time Is Officially Getting His Own Netflix Series

Just about everyone loves a good antihero. Morally gray protagonists who are more than willing to engage in decidedly unheroic actions for the greater good have become more and more popular on-screen as audiences seek out more challenging and interesting characters. Comics, in particular, have birthed some of the most beloved leads of this kind, from Marvel's Punisher, Deadpool, and Wolverine, to John Constantine from DC, and Todd McFarlane's legendary Image Comics icon, Spawn. Just as it once introduced viewers to Jon Bernthal's rendition of Frank Castle, Netflix is now bringing another storied antihero to life from the pages of an independent classic that's been around for over 40 years.

The streamer has officially announced a new animated adaptation of Matt Wagner's long-running Dark Horse Comics noir title, Grendel. Accompanying the news is a new image giving a taste of what the series' gritty portrayal of New York could look like once it hits the screen, with the vigilante himself standing front and center. Bobak Esfarjani, the Emmy-winning producer of Apple TV's breakout horror comedy hit Widow's Bay, among other things, has been tapped as writer, showrunner, and executive producer. This project will be the latest addition to Netflix's ever-growing catalog of adult animation, which, to this point, has taken on games like Devil May Cry, Castlevania, and League of Legends and even ventured into the cinematic realm of King Kong with Skull Island.

First published in 1982, Grendel follows Hunter Rose, a successful author who becomes a masked vigilante after the love of his life is horrifically murdered. He dedicates his life to seeking vengeance, tearing through "street gangs, the elite, and New York City’s supernatural underworld" to find and put an end to her killer. During his quest, however, the opportunity to pursue a real life arises, forcing him to make a choice that could either save him or inevitably turn him into the very monster he's been hunting the whole time. Wagner issued an official statement praising the new project as a faithful embrace of his original comic from the storytelling to the action, writing:

"It’s incredibly exciting to see my creation finally make this leap to the animated screen! Netflix’s dynamic new series retains the source material’s dark adult themes and also brings a fresh and thrilling approach to the narrative. This is Grendel as I’ve always wanted to see the character portrayed — a hyper-kinetic level of action, bracing explosions of violence, and a poignant, engaging storyline.”

Handling the animation for Netflix's Grendel series is Bobbypills, the studio best known for their work on James Gunn's DC Creature Commandos series. They're familiar partners to Netflix, having previously been involved with Adi Shankar's Ubisoft mash-up Captain Laserhawk: A Blood Dragon Remix. Chris Tongue, Tim Wiesch, and Jay Komas also serve as executive producers for Dark Horse Entertainment, joining Lydia Antonini and Wagner. In a separate statement, Esfarjani expressed his gratitude and excitement to the entire team working with him on the comic adaptation, adding:

“Being able to bring a character as iconic as Grendel to life has been a true thrill. Having the support of Matt Wagner, my great EPs, and the awesome team of Netflix, has made it all the more exciting, and partnering with Bobbypills Studio has made it all a true joy.”

Stay tuned here at Collider for more on Netflix's Grendel adaptation as it comes together.

#3359. ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott’s Towering Performance as a Dying Actor Can’t Overcome AIDS-Movie Awards Bait Clichés

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 5, 2026 during the 2026 Telluride Film Festival. Focus Features will release the film in theaters Friday, November 20.]

There’s no question Andrew Scott, the 49-year-old Irish actor, has earned his position as one of the finest contemporary actors going. He’s in demand, but choosing wisely, and in roles that slyly play off his own status as an out gay man (a rare thing indeed) but with something off-center beneath, often a secret. He played Tom Ripley, one even more sociopathic than Matt Damon’s own iconically calculating Adonis, to devastating effect in the sinister Netflix series “Ripley,” there more explicitly grappling with the Patricia Highsmith character’s ambiguous (but was it?) sexuality. He played the Hot Priest who turned down a chance at heterosexual, secular love in “Fleabag,” of course, and starred in “All of Us Strangers” as a lonely adult orphan living in a glittering tower, bracing himself for romantic intimacy with Paul Mescal. Related Stories Jim Cummings Wakes Up to a Post-One-Night-Stand Crisis in ‘DISC’ — Watch the Short ‘Artificial’ Trailer: Andrew Garfield Stuns in Luca Guadagnino’s Sharp, Shocking, Funny Portrayal of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman

I also saw him playing up to nine roles in Anton Chekhov’s “Vanya” onstage in New York City last year as men and women of all sorts, showing an actor who can shimmy between genders and across ranges. He has the unmistakable warmth of someone you should trust, but with intrigue behind the curtain of many of his performances to suggest that maybe you shouldn’t. He’s that good.

Scott has now taken on what will, to this point, I suppose, go down as “the role of a lifetime” in director Simon Stone’s rueful, pained, and unremarkable new film drama “Elsinore” as Scottish actor Ian Charleson, who died of HIV/AIDS complications while portraying Hamlet at the National Theatre in London in 1990. Charleson’s story is unlikely to be one most are familiar with. Even the most public of deaths among the most publicly gay of people often still remain in hiding, though Charleson wasn’t out himself. He resisted pressures from his inner circle to announce his disease amid a stage run that miraculously lasted 24 performances. Actors then were afraid of damaging their reputations. It’s not that different now, even as many advancements have made HIV/AIDS feel locally like a plague of the past.

A blond-headed Scott throws himself valiantly into the role of Charleson with the urgency and commitment of any of his best work, but the problem isn’t his: It’s that the movie surrounding him dulls the greatness of his performance with its conventional storytelling, and over-complication in post. “Elsinore” is one of those movies where you can feel the filmmaker — here, Stone, known for both stage and screen — actively laboring to “open up the play” with the opportunities of film. But “Elsinore” was never a play. Instead, it’s a movie where every emotional beat worth lingering on, especially Charleson’s swan-song performances as Hamlet, is churned into a frenzied montage of editing that won’t let the material take a breath. Or the audience sink in.

Charleson played an Olympian athlete in the Best Picture-winning 1981 film “Chariots of Fire,” and an Anglican priest in the next year’s Best Picture topper, “Gandhi.” That was after playing an outré bisexual in the 1978 film “Jubilee,” directed by his former lover, the very openly gay director Derek Jarman, who died of AIDS in 1994. Aside from a handful of film credits, including one alluded to in “Elsinore” as Dario Argento’s giallo “Opera,” Charleson otherwise kept to the stage. Scott’s Charleson at one point in this film opines about how much more satisfying stage work is for an actor without an editor there to chop you up to pieces.

Stone, working from a screenplay by Stephen Beresford (himself a playwright), does not follow his protagonist’s lead. Every thoughtful consideration of Kaposi’s sarcoma lesions, or the retching of blood into buckets under the care of dutiful practitioner Dr. Margaret Johnson (Olivia Colman) to show the terrible realities of the disease, is whipped into what feels like a feature-length trailer. The best scenes out of the “Hamlet” production detailed here are tossed into a rushed montage near the movie’s end that gives us no sense of what we are promised is a performance of enormity. (The play in 1990 was directed by Richard Eyre, later the filmmaker behind features like the campy diva battle “Notes on a Scandal.” He’s played in “Elsinore” by Johnny Flynn.)

A couple of things are going on: “Elsinore” triggers in a watchful gay viewer’s senses the signifiers of what would be the AIDS awards-bait movie of serious gravitas. Tom Hanks’ Oscar-winning performance in “Philadelphia.” Ed Harris in “The Hours.” Everyone who came out of the cringey “Dallas Buyers Club” with Academy Awards in 2014. There are others, though more lost to time. We become suspicious of this device, especially when paired with great acting. Is HIV/AIDS being exploited in the package of a would-be Oscar hit? Or are we showing young queer audiences how it was, how we got to where we are, and how where that is still isn’t perfect? It can be both, but the structure of “Elsinore” tips toward the former.

Then, there’s a veritable, cheeky who’s-who of British gay literati and luminaries lingering about “Elsinore’s” 1989 London milieu that’s irresistible in theory, but often drab in execution. There’s Eyre, of course, and Jarman (David Dawson, as excellent and tender and wounded here as he was in his screen breakthrough “My Policeman”). The afterburn of his relationship with Charleson lingers affectingly, though. After some drinks, he invites Charleson home, but they instead part with one of those tacit kisses shared by people who once loved each other but can’t make it work anymore. There’s too much history here. The lingering scorches of Charleson’s secret affairs and friendships with various (and out) men make for the best parts of “Elsinore,” but there’s no life to the telling. (Joe Locke plays a young man also ailing in Johnson’s AIDS clinic alongside Charleson.)

The pallid grayness of Mike Eley’s cinematography is probably supposed to mimic the finality of HIV/AIDS taking hold, but there’s no passion aesthetically to counterbalance what becomes absolute misery onscreen to watch. I’m not in the business of comparing one gay social drama to another, but Robin Campillo’s 2017 Cannes-winning French drama “Beats Per Minute” imbued an albeit more activist-oriented story of ACT UP fighting against AIDS suppression in Paris with such heat and spectacle. Watching someone die of AIDS in a room becomes a bore unless anyone is given a reason to keep on living.

That reason is, of course, supposed to be Charleson’s performance in “Hamlet,” which is relegated to a whirlwind sequence at the movie’s end after many pained rehearsals where he refused to drop out (and where Johnson encouraged him to). Scott has a mesmerizing hold on his scenes, and he’s compelling to watch in his repartee with Colman as Johnson, who treated the disease at a time when it was most stigmatized. She named her groundbreaking HIV testing clinic after him; that’s how much he impacted her. We are told how much Charleson mattered to people, but never shown it. Which unfortunately shuffles off “Elsinore,” named after the Danish town where “Hamlet” was set and where its main character died, off to the realm of HIV/AIDS movies seeking prestige over deep feeling.

“Elsinore” premiered at the 2026 Telluride Film Festival. Focus Features releases it starting November 20.

#3358. macOS 27.3 includes new privacy controls for Full Disk Access and more

With today’s new macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this.

In a post on its developer website last month, Apple said some developers are “using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems.” As such, it said that it would “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

In macOS 27.2, “Device Control and Data Access” is a unified toggle in System Settings, where Apple says that apps with that level of access can “view and send email, edit contacts and photos, monitor your keyboard, track websites, record your screen, control any app on your Mac, and more.”

In macOS 27.3, Apple is splitting “Device Control and Data Access” into two categories:

For the latter, users will be able to specify which apps an automation tool can access rather than granting it unrestricted control. For instance, you could give an app access to the Mail app, but not Messages.

macOS 27.3 also adds an option for users to require an app to request permission every time it needs access, rather than granting it access indefinitely.

Apple is also introducing a new menu bar indicator that will provide additional transparency when an app is controlling another app with System and App Protection Override. This is designed to let users know when an automation tool is interacting with apps and information in the background.

Crucially, Apple isn’t removing the ability to give an app Full Disk Access. If you deem it necessary, you can still give an app Full Disk Access. However, Apple is redesigning the approval process to make the implications of that decision more obvious.

macOS 27.3 will display a more detailed explanation about the protections being bypassed and the types of personal information that could be exposed.

Users can also choose to grant an app access to specific folders instead of their entire Mac. For example, an app that only needs to work with files in a particular folder won’t get unrestricted access to everything else.

Any app you’ve already given Full Disk Access will still have that access. Previously granted permissions will remain in effect, and those apps will continue functioning as they do today without any approval required.

Apple has published a new support document detailing the Full Disk Access updates.

macOS 27.3 now warns you before giving an app full disk accessThat warning prompt is pretty scary! pic.twitter.com/J2qCKVWJRx

Apple says the underlying APIs aren’t changing, but developers will need to update their apps to account for situations where users grant limited access rather than unrestricted permissions.

Finally, Apple says developers of backup apps and assistive technologies can request entitlements that allow them to maintain the same experience for new installations as before macOS 27.3. Apple has already identified popular apps that rely on these permissions, and those apps will continue working as expected without requiring an entitlement.

Developers can read more on Apple’s Developer website.

#3357. 10 Most Memorable Jujutsu Kaisen Characters

Few shonen series have introduced as many unforgettable characters as Jujutsu Kaisen. From exceptionally powerful sorcerers and terrifying curses to students struggling to find their place in a dangerous world, Gege Akutami's manga has no shortage of personalities who leave a lasting impression. Some stand out because of their incredible abilities, while others become fan favorites through their relationships, personal struggles, or the emotional weight of their stories.

Of course, being memorable doesn't necessarily mean being heroic or even likable. Several of Jujutsu Kaisen's most recognizable characters are responsible for its cruelest moments, while others remain beloved despite the shortcomings of their storylines. Whether they changed the course of the narrative, delivered some of its most devastating moments, or simply became impossible for fans to forget, these characters helped make Jujutsu Kaisen the phenomenon it is today.

Jujutsu Kaisen introduces Mahito, an undeniably hateable villain, who is almost universally disliked by viewers. From his early appearances, Mahito is crafted to leave a lasting impression with each twisted action, becoming progressively more despicable. His manipulation of Junpei solidifies him as one of the most loathsome characters, but his defining moment comes during the Shibuya Incident arc.

During the height of this arc, Mahito had killed thousands of humans, including one of the most loved characters from the series, Nanami, and left the fate of the female lead, Nobara, hanging. The satisfaction of seeing Yuji finally end Mahito’s reign of terror makes this a pivotal moment, with Mahito brought to his lowest point, solidifying his place as one of the series’ most memorable villains for all the wrong reasons.

The deuteragonist, Megumi Fushiguro, is easily mistaken as the series protagonist instead, as the series intricately weaves many key narratives around him. Megumi possesses the traits commonly associated with shonen lead character, such as hidden abilities, a powerful lineage, and a father whose actions have deeply influenced his life. Unlike some other characters, Megumi has a clear and compelling motive for becoming a sorcerer, making him an intriguing figure to follow.

Here's a comprehensive guide of what happened to Jujutsu Kaisen's major characters in both the original series and the spin-off manga.

Additionally, Megumi has also become the subject of a lighthearted joke among fans, who note how quick he is to summon his trump card, Mahoraga, even in situations that don't seem to warrant it. His significance is further emphasized when he becomes a vessel for Sukuna, solidifying his importance in the series. With all these elements, there’s little doubt that Megumi will remain one of the most memorable characters in Jujutsu Kaisen.

While the Shonen genre often struggles with the portrayal of female characters, Jujutsu Kaisen takes this issue to another level. Nobara Kugisaki, the female lead, initially seemed poised to become one of the series’ strongest characters. However, as the narrative progressed, she was sidelined for almost half of the story. Her fate during the Shibuya arc was left ambiguous, and with no return in sight, fans had even accepted that perhaps the character is indeed dead.

Near the end of the series, it’s revealed that Nobara is alive, but by then, the opportunity to craft a compelling arc for her had long passed. Her portrayal feels oddly incomplete, and while she remains a memorable character, it’s for reasons that highlight the series’ missed potential in developing its female lead. Still, there's no doubt that Nobara ranks among Jujutsu Kaisen's strongest women.

Jujutsu Kaisen features several villains, but few are as compelling or memorable as Suguru Geto. The Hidden Inventory arc, which details Geto’s tragic descent into villainy, weaves a poignant and emotionally charged narrative centered around his deep bond with Gojo Satoru. The shock of seeing Geto, once allied with the strongest sorcerer, fall to the dark side and ultimately meet a heartbreaking end at the hands of his best friend makes his arc all the more impactful.

What makes Geto’s story even more intriguing is the revelation that Kenjaku, a millennium-old sorcerer, has taken over his body. Kenjaku’s centuries-old plans come to life, adding layers of intrigue and mystery to the narrative. With his extensive experience as a cursed user, Kenjaku emerges as one of the series’ most fascinating characters, arguably even more so than Sukuna, therefore it is a shame that the series fails to address this character's origin.

The strength of the characters in Jujutsu Kaisen is measured by the amount of cursed energy the characters possess. Therefore, for a character such as Toji, who possesses zero cursed energy, it instantly puts him at a rank of his own. With no cursed energy, Toji is blessed with a side effect that improves all of his senses with superhuman strength. His portrayal leans toward villainy, largely due to his complex relationship with the Zenin family, which led him down a dark path.

One of Toji’s most defining moments is when he nearly killed Gojo Satoru, the strongest sorcerer of the modern era, who possesses a vast amount of cursed energy and the Six Eyes. While Toji was essentially killed in this battle, he has become memorable for almost killing Gojo while not many could even touch the strongest sorcerer.

Yuta Okkotsu, often seen by fans as a more fitting protagonist than Yuji Itadori, does indeed meet all the criteria of a Shōnen protagonist. His portrayal in Jujutsu Kaisen 0 is especially compelling, largely due to the well-crafted narrative that surrounds him. Blessed with immense cursed energy, Yuta is not only able to hold his own in any battle but often comes out victorious. Jujutsu Kaisen 0's manga was also a prototype for the series as a whole, meaning Yuta was originally the series' protagonist before Yuji.

What sets Yuta apart is his unique cursed technique, which allows him to copy the abilities of others and even wield their weapons against them. This versatility, combined with his raw power, makes him a standout character. Arguably, Yuta is one of the strongest characters in Jujutsu Kaisen, and in a heavy-action battle series such as this, it already gives him an edge to be memorable.

Watching Jujutsu Kaisen for the first time will leave an impression on the viewers as if Yuji Itadori isn't the main character of Jujutsu Kaisen. The portrayal of Yuji isn't what is generally expected of a Shōnen hero, with the character even lacking a main motive to enter the world of the sorcerer. It was only after an incident that Yuji was pushed into this new world but since, Yuji has made a remarkable journey.

Born with an extraordinary body, Yuji was able to harbor Sukuna inside him and since then, has done his best what is expected of him. Over time, the series flirts with the "chosen one" trope, hinting that Yuji may share a deeper connection with Sukuna. However, it’s not just this potential destiny that defines him—it’s his inherent uniqueness. This quality makes Yuji not only a standout character in Jujutsu Kaisen but also a refreshing presence within the Shonen genre.

Essentially, Jujutsu Kaisen is Shōnen Jump's most battle-focused manga, so the popularity of the characters is rooted in how strong the characters are. Ryomen Sukuna, the series's main antagonist, is arguably the strongest character of the series, with a scale of power so high that even Gojo Satoru, deemed as the strongest, didn't stand a chance. It was only through the cumulative damage inflicted by various sorcerers and the fact that Sukuna had not yet regained his full strength that he was eventually brought down.

Jujutsu Kaisen has many sorcerers with overwhelming powers and insane cursed techniques, but only a few can be called the strongest in the franchise.

Every action Sukuna took throughout the series was driven solely by his own ambitions, and in the process, he sacrificed thousands without a second thought. Fans initially believed that Sukuna would play a role similar to Kurama from Naruto, aiding Yuji in some way. However, Sukuna’s purpose was singularly his own. Sukuna's ruthless nature and overwhelming prowess make him one of the series' most memorable and unique characters.

Amidst the characters wielding incredible supernatural powers and villains with centuries-old schemes, Kento Nanami stands out as the most relatable figure in Jujutsu Kaisen. His grounded presence introduces a sense of realism that naturally draws viewers to him. Unlike many characters with lofty dreams and aspirations, Nanami simply desires to live a good, uneventful life.

As Yuji Itadori's mentor, Nanami brings a heartwarming dynamic to the series, forming what is arguably its best duo. His reluctance to fully embrace the life of a sorcerer, due to the profession’s inescapable ties to death, makes his eventual fate all the more heartbreaking. Written with a relatable realism that resonates with Jujutsu Kaisen fans, Nanami is one of the most memorable and well-crafted characters in Jujutsu Kaisen.

Satoru Gojo, the strongest sorcerer of the modern era, also known as the 'Honored One' or simply, 'The Strongest,' goes by many names, and it’s hardly an exaggeration to say that his popularity is more than the whole series itself. From the series' commencement, the series depicted Gojo as the strongest, and since then, the fleets of the strongest sorcerers have been unachievable. Gojo's portrayal in Jujutsu Kaisen has become such an iconic element that his influence has affected fans to act in real life. Jujutsu Kaisen's creator also famously does not like Gojo, and has joked about it several times.

When Gojo was first sealed inside the prison realm, an X account (formerly Twitter) was dedicated solely to counting the real-time duration of his confinement. Whereas, when Gojo met his demise in the battle against Sukuna, fans in Chile even held a real-life memorial in his honor, tied to the series' promotion. These actions from fans demonstrate just how deeply Gojo resonates, arguably making him the most memorable character in Jujutsu Kaisen, perhaps even more iconic than the series itself.

Jujutsu Kaisen is a Japanese anime and manga series created by Gege Akutami. The story is set in a world where Cursed Spirits, born from negative human emotions, prey on humanity. It follows high school student Yuji Itadori as he becomes entangled in the world of Jujutsu Sorcery after swallowing a cursed talisman—Ryomen Sukuna's finger—and becomes the host for one of the most powerful curses. Yuji joins the Tokyo Metropolitan Magic Technical College to learn how to combat curses while searching for the remaining fingers of Sukuna to exorcise him permanently.

#3356. Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone

The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first. Personally, I’ve had my eye on the Google variant, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—and recently I finally took the plunge. I thought I’d done my research to know how different having a foldable phone would be, but I still had a bit to learn. Here are some of the things I wish I’ve learned along the way after making the jump to foldables.

One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed. And there’s a good reason for that: The larger screen while open has exactly the same 1.41:1 aspect ratio as the smaller screen while closed. This has a ripple effect on how every app you use looks and feels—and whether you like Apple’s approach is largely a matter of personal preference.

Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open. On the outer screen, apps are a little less wide than on my old phone, but there’s plenty of space for reading books or articles on the inner screen.

I like the tall, thin display personally because it feels easier to reach buttons with my thumb, and the wider display is better for reading. However, this approach can occasionally result in some odd app layouts. Not every app is designed for tablets, especially on Android, and shifting the aspect ratio between the inner and outer display sometimes means re-rendering or even restarting an app entirely to load properly.

The iPhone Duo has a more consistent aspect ratio and general feel between the inner and outer display, but it comes at the cost of a really wide phone. Neither approach is better or worse on its own, but it might be worth going to a local store to get your hands on the phone you’re thinking about before buying.

For years, the screens on most smartphones have been made of increasingly tough and scratch-resistant glass. So tough that you might not even need a screen protector anymore. On a foldable phone, that can be true of the outside display, but it’s very much not when it comes to the inner, foldable display.

Screens might be foldable, but the strong, durable glass that makes your phone so scratch-resistant isn’t. No matter what foldable phone you use, the covering on the inner display will be more flexible, and thus softer. Apple uses a nano-texture polymer film that can be replaced, but the film on most foldable phones cannot. That means if they get damaged or scratched, those marks will be there for the life of your phone.

If you (like me) haven’t considered a screen protector in a while, it might be time to try one again, at least for the inner display. It’s also worth keeping in mind how rough you plan to be with your phone. Construction sites or factories might not be the best home for a foldable phone you plan to open a lot, but an office job should be a bit safer.

Similar to the screen protector issue, cases can be more of a headache. Most rigid cases will come in two pieces, and the piece that covers the outer display can be shockingly minimal—barely more than a frame, for some of the cases I looked at. A poorly made case can be brittle or pop off more easily, so it’s more important to get a high-quality one.

If you like to use your phone case as your wallet, it’s also important to be wary of cases that aren’t specifically designed for your model of phone (and maybe some that are). A lot of wallet cases are built to unfold to reveal your phone’s screen on one side, and your cards and ID on the other. But depending on how your foldable phone unfolds, it could be awkward to reach the inner screen.

The hinge also introduces more spaces for dust and debris to get into your phone. Despite the extra moving parts and gaps, most foldable phones still offer the now-standard IP68 dust and water resistance rating. That mainly applies to what can get inside and damage the components inside your phone. It’s still possible for hair and dirt to get gummed up in any pinchable spaces, so look out for any case that might provide even more nooks for dust to collect in.

I’ve set up most of my apps how I like them by now, but when I first got my foldable phone, I had to revisit some settings I thought I was done messing with. One of the most notable examples was my ebook apps: I was previously using a single-column, medium-font layout, but it looked ridiculous on the inner display. After switching to a two-column layout, it not only felt more natural, but a lot like reading a regular book.

Similarly, there were some uses for my calendar app that got a whole lot more useful. I’ve never really been able to use anything other than either the one-day or Schedule view if I want to make out anything, but on the inner screen, I can finally look at my week at a glance. But that meant tweaking some things—like showing reminders, which fit naturally amid my events in Schedule view, but become a cluttered mess when I saw 14 different reminders to take my meds at once in the Week view.

Most apps do a decent job of automatically adjusting to different screen sizes, but I found a few outliers that I had to figure out myself. As an example, Google Docs would default to a view with extremely tiny text when I first started using it. It took me a bit to figure out that this was due to a “Print layout” toggle in the document’s settings. This is, for some reason, enabled by default when opening a document on the larger inner screen. It can take some time to learn the eccentricities of all your apps, but it’s worth poking around when you can.

I know, it sounds so obvious, right? The outer screen is the one you’ll use most often, so how could you forget about it? But when you unfold the inner screen, the outer one is still useful in some surprising ways that I hadn’t even considered until I went poking around in some of my apps.

One of the most adorable examples is the Made You Look feature in the Pixel’s Camera app. When unfolded, you can take a picture using the rear camera and see a preview like normal, while the outer screen shows silly animations to capture the attention of a baby or toddler that you want to look into the camera. Admittedly, this is an older feature, but it’s a clever one. For adults, you can also use the outer display to get a selfie preview while using the rear-facing camera.

The outer screen is also just better for some things. YouTube is one of the few apps that has a unique layout designed for a partially folded screen, with the video playing on the tilted-up portion of the screen, and video controls on the bottom portion.

However, in my experience, it was a lot nicer to watch a YouTube video by just propping up the outer screen by unfolding the phone a bit, like a kickstand. My Pixel even detected when YouTube was in full-screen mode on the outer display and would be more forgiving of unfolding the phone without switching to the inner screen. The phone anticipated I might just want to prop up the smaller screen, which I thought was a nice touch.

#3355. Skydance to Combine Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios as One Big Studio

The corporate shakeups keep coming at Skydance, this time to the TV department. Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios are being combined as one big studio under Skydance, with WB’s Channing Dungey and Paramount’s Matt Thunell serving as presidents of the combined studio.

The new studio, which officially launches in early 2027 (the two entities will keep operating independently until then), will be known as Warner Bros. Television Studios. The entire studio will report to George Cheeks, co-chair and Chief Content Officer of Skydance TV. As previously announced, Dungey also serves as Chair of Skydance Global Cable Media, with oversight over all 50+ WB Discovery and Paramount cable brands. Related Stories IDA Documentary Awards 2026 Nominations: ‘You Can See Everything,’ ‘Concrete Land,’ and More Earn Nods A24’s TV Division Is Quietly Having as Strong a Year as Its Film Team

Together, Dungey and Thunell will lead all of scripted and unscripted programming, overseeing all creative departments. They will also oversee BET Studios and Warner Bros. International Television Production’s studios around the world.

CBS Studios will continue to operate independently, headed by President David Stapf, who also reports to Cheeks. CBS Studios International, Skydance Sports Entertainment and See It Now Studios will operate under the CBS Studios umbrella.

The new Warner Bros. Television Studios will be home to more than 120 active television series and some of the industry’s biggest global franchises, including “Harry Potter and The Philosopher’s Stone” (HBO), “The Pitt” (HBO Max), “Ted Lasso” (Apple TV), “Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage” (CBS), “Reacher” (Prime Video), “Marshals” (CBS), “Landman” (Paramount+), “Emily in Paris” (Netflix) and the upcoming series “Neuromancer” (Apple TV).

Yesterday, Skydance made some big changes to its film side of the business, appointing Don Granger and Kira Goldberg to lead Paramount’s Motion Picture Group and Jesse Ehrman to lead Warner Bros. Pictures. It also recently shook up DC Studios, with James Gunn and Peter Safran exiting and giving way to Jeremy Latcham.

“Bringing together two of the industry’s most prolific television studios creates a formidable creative engine, uniting extraordinary talent, resources, acclaimed programming and iconic franchises with the global scale to compete at the highest level. With Channing and Matt at the helm, we have two exceptional leaders who understand what it takes to empower creative talent, foster bold ideas and deliver programming that resonates with audiences everywhere,” Cheeks said in a statement. “Alongside CBS Studios, led by the incomparable David Stapf, Warner Bros. Television Studios gives us two world-class studios, with the breadth, depth and creative ambition to deliver for Skydance platforms and third-party partners across the industry.”

“Matt has extraordinary creative instincts, and a deep understanding of great storytelling. I couldn’t ask for a better partner as we bring these storied studios together,” Dungey said in a statement. “We have a unique opportunity to create something truly special for our creative partners and audiences around the world. I’m very excited to begin this new chapter.”

Thunell said, “Channing is one of the most accomplished and respected executives in our industry, with an extraordinary track record of building successful businesses, developing enduring partnerships and delivering some of television’s most acclaimed programming. Ever since our time together at Netflix, I’ve hoped we’d have the opportunity to work together again, and I’m thrilled that day has finally come. We’re bringing an unmatched roster of talent under one roof, building on the remarkable legacies of two storied studios. The possibilities ahead are extraordinary, and I couldn’t be more excited to partner with Channing to champion the ambitions of our creative talent and bring exceptional stories to audiences around the world.”

#3354. iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

In today’s iOS 27.3 beta release, Apple is introducing two changes for iPhone Duo users. Most notably, it adds a new face recognition option that lets you unlock your iPhone Duo by looking at it.

Apple is also adding an option to have your iPhone Duo lock when you close it.

You can enable the new option to unlock your iPhone Duo with the front camera in Settings, under Touch ID & Passcode, after updating to iOS 27.3. When enabled, your iPhone Duo will unlock after recognizing your face.

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

This isn’t Face ID. This new option on iPhone Duo uses the front camera on the outer iPhone Duo display to recognize your face. The iPhone Duo doesn’t have the hardware needed for Face ID.

Because this isn’t as secure as Face ID, Touch ID, or your passcode, Apple has implemented a few guardrails. First, the setting only works to unlock your iPhone Duo. To use Apple Pay, access your passwords, unlock apps, and do other things that require authentication, you’ll have to use Touch ID or enter your passcode.

This face recognition feature also has a time-based limitation. After 45 minutes of inactivity, you have to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. That is, if you go 45 minutes without unlocking your iPhone Duo, the facial recognition feature is disabled until you enter your passcode or use Touch ID.

Finally, this new feature also doesn’t work when using the iPhone Duo unfolded. When unfolded, you still have to use Touch ID or your passcode to unlock the device.

Second, iOS 27.3 adds an option to lock your iPhone Duo when you close it. You can enable this in Settings, under Display & Brightness. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold, rather than transition from the inner display to the outer display.

Many iPhone Duo users (myself included) have said Apple should do this. Personally, I’ve been using a shortcut to mimic this behavior, but I’m glad to see that Apple has listened to user feedback and added a default setting for it.
