#3353. The Unexpected History of 'Black Friday'

Since the 1950s, Black Friday—once simply known as "the day after Thanksgiving"—has grown into a quasi-holiday in the United States marked by steep discounts, ceaseless shopping, and occasional violence. But more recently, Black Friday has also metastasized. It's not a day anymore. It's a week, a month, a veritable state of mind. (Speaking of which, check out Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage. We got all the deals, baby!)

While pre-dawn trips to the mall are waning as online shopping grows, in-person shopping on Black Friday is still a big deal in the U.S.—it’s estimated that around 80 million Americans visited a brick-and-mortar store on Black Friday in 2025. But how did Black Friday come about, and what does it all mean?

“Black Friday” in the United States originally referred to the start of the Panic of 1869, when the collapse of the price of gold devastated the national economy. “Black Friday” as a description of the day after Thanksgiving dates back to 1951; the term first appeared in the journal Factory Management and Maintenance, where it referred to the number of employees who skipped work on the day after Thanksgiving. Around the same time, the police in Philadelphia and Rochester started informally using “Black Friday” to describe the traffic and crowds that appeared in their cities as shoppers hit the stores on the day after Thanksgiving. The phrase gradually caught on. It was picked up by national press in 1975 when the New York Times used "Black Friday" specifically to describe the day after Thanksgiving and the shopping and sales it brings.

But even before it had a name, Black Friday was a thing. The day after Thanksgiving has been known by merchants as the start of the shopping season since the late 1800s. By the early 20th century, retailers sponsored Thanksgiving Day parades that traditionally ended with an appearance by Santa Claus, as if to say, “Now it’s time to shop for Christmas.” By unspoken agreement among retailers, Christmas-themed advertisements rarely appeared before Thanksgiving in our grandparents’ day. This informal bargain obviously no longer applies.

Referring to a day as “black” traditionally denotes a period of calamity or tragedy, leading some to suggest different names for the day. In the early 1960s, Philadelphia merchants suggested “Big Friday,” a name which did not catch on, leaving retailers with the weak explanation that the “black” in Black Friday refers to the black ink denoting profits in a ledger. Oft-repeated lore suggests that retailers are "in the red" all year, and only start making an annual profit at the end of the year, but big retail chains generally make money all year long.

A more modern issue with the name is that Black Friday sales now last for days or even weeks, beginning in early to mid-November and bleeding over into the following Saturday, Sunday, “Cyber Monday,” Tuesday, and beyond, leading people to say things like, “Do you want to go Black Friday shopping this Sunday?” So far, alternative names like “Five-Day Frenzy” and “The day I get to trample someone to save $8 on a Nespresso” haven’t caught on. But here’s hoping.

Beginning around 2010, an insatiable thirst for profits led many retailers to push the start of Black Friday shopping to Thursday (aka Thanksgiving Day). Kmart opened Thanksgiving morning. Toys R Us opened that night. By 2011, Walmart was opening its doors at 10 p.m. on Thursday. The trend led to widespread backlash, with many Americans appalled that employees were forced to work on Thanksgiving or angry that consumerism was encroaching upon a holiday meant to celebrate colonialism. By 2021, most major retailers had relented and elected to remain closed on Thanksgiving.

The term “Cyber Monday” describes the boost in online retail sales on the Monday after Thanksgiving, sparked by workers returning to the office and getting right to online shopping. The term first appeared on Nov. 28, 2005, in a Shop.org press release entitled “'Cyber Monday’ Quickly Becoming One of the Biggest Online Shopping Days of the Year," which may be the most influential press release ever written. Since its early 2000s birth, Cyber Monday has become the biggest online shopping day of the year. Americans spent $14.25 billion online on Cyber Monday 2025, according to Adobe Analytics. So is Cyber Monday bigger than Black Friday? Retailers really don't care: Analysts now tend to mash everything into the category of "Black Friday–Cyber Monday" (or even "Cyber Week").

If all this naked consumerism makes you a little squeamish, you're not alone. Anti-consumerists have named the day after Thanksgiving “Buy Nothing Day,” which you can celebrate by doing charity work, cutting up your credit cards, or simply not purchasing anything. Pioneered by artist Ted Dave and popularized by Adbusters magazine, the first Buy Nothing Day was celebrated in Canada in 1992.

It’s hard to measure the success of the alternative holiday. Both online and brick-and-mortar retail sales have increased sharply since 1992, suggesting Buy Nothing Day’s effect is negligible. On the other hand, maybe big retailers are losing millions because someone on Bluesky reminded you not to shop. Sure.

Depending on how you measure it, Black Friday has resulted in between one and 17 deaths. Jdimytai Damour is the only person killed directly due to a Black Friday sale: The 34-year-old worker was trampled to death by a surging crowd at a Long Island Walmart on Black Friday in 2008. If you include car accidents, shootings, retail worker suicides, and fatal heart attacks, Black Friday’s death toll balloons to 17, with 128 reported injuries.

Black Friday violence has even inspired a horror flick: Eli Roth's 2023 holiday-themed slasher Thanksgiving opens with a hilariously brutal Black Friday riot at a big box store, setting off a chain of events that involve a lot of people being murdered by a dude in a Pilgrim mask.

I mean, yeah, of course. Critics of Black Friday point out that there are arguably better times to buy a new TV (like the week before the Super Bowl), not to mention plenty of other goods. Savings from Black Friday shopping are often illusory—big-ticket “doorbuster” items generally sell out quickly, leaving behind goods that are, by and large, priced the same as they would be at any other time of year. Some retailers even mark up products ahead of Black Friday so the discounts look bigger. If you're buying online, your browser history, location, and cart contents can tweak the prices you see on Black Friday, as they can on any other day.

Yet despite protest holidays, the unpleasantness of shopping when stores are overcrowded, and the frustration of hunting for bargains that often aren't that great to begin with, Black Friday stubbornly remains an unofficial holiday, celebrated by over 100 million Americans in one way or another. What that says about our country's relationship with capitalism is unclear, but personally, I’m going to continue my own day-after-Thanksgiving tradition of eating pie for breakfast and thinking about going for a walk, but then watching The Quick and the Dead instead. I'm not protesting anything; I just don't need the hassle.

#3352. ’Pride and Prejudice’s 10-Part Spin-Off Is the Perfect Binge Before Its Christmas Special

Taylor Vollman is a contributor at Collider. She has long quipped, “T.V. is my name, TV is my game.” Fortuitous initials aside, at the heart of a tired joke is a simple truth — she has a lifelong passion for television. And along with it, an affinity for movies, music and pop culture.

In a childhood time capsule, she had listed Friends, PB&J Otter, and Days of Our Lives among her favorite shows. But her tastes have not narrowed with age. Her viewing habits span TV Land classics, network hits, buzzy reality shows and streamer critical darlings.

Hoping to merge this passion with her love of writing, Taylor earned a bachelor’s in media arts and design with a minor in film studies from James Madison University. After working in marketing for years, she wanted to sharpen her skills and went on to graduate with a master’s in journalism from Georgetown University. Taylor has since pursued entertainment writing and reporting.

Jane Austen is a preeminent romance author, with an impressive catalog of novels that are still relevant centuries later. Pride and Prejudice was her second novel published in 1813 and continues to be her most successful, repeatedly adapted for stage, screen, and page. It documents the at-times fraught romance of Elizabeth Bennett and Mr. Darcy, who must overcome misconceptions and differing stations in life to find happiness. But BritBox’s breakout hit of 2026 shifted its focus, instead turning to Elizabeth’s overlooked middle sister, Mary.

The Other Bennet Sister is based on Janice Hadlow’s 2020 novel of the same name, adapted for screen by Sarah Quintrell. Ella Bruccoleri stars as the socially awkward, but endearing titular character as she ventures to define herself separately from her critical family. With just 10, roughly half-hour-long episodes, it is the perfect weekend binge ahead of the upcoming release of its Christmas special.

As the last unmarried sibling, The Other Bennet Sister follows Mary Bennet as she sets out on a journey of self-discovery and romance. She is the bespectacled middle sister of Pride and Prejudice’s Elizabeth Bennet, often finding herself as the odd-woman out in their sibling set of five. Lacking the same wit, beauty, and coordination as her siblings, her negative self-image is reinforced by the highly critical Mrs. Bennet (Ruth Jones). Not only does she vocalize her worry that Mary could hinder proposals for her other daughters, but she actively thwarts perfectly serviceable matches. Mary explains her central issue in the opening lines of the series, which mimic the opening lines of the book. “It is a sad fact of life that if a young woman is unlucky enough to come into the world without expectations, she had better do all she can to ensure that she is beautiful. To be poor and handsome is misfortune enough, but to be penniless and plain is a hard fate, indeed,” says Bruccoleri.

With the assistance of some helpful extended family members and newfound friends, she journeys to London for work before finding herself caught up in a love triangle between Laurie Davidson as Mr. Ryder and Dónal Finn as Mr. Tom Hayward. Other Pride and Prejudice characters continue to reappear, including Charlotte Lucas (Anna Fenton-Garvey) and Mr. Collins (Ryan Sampson). Mary finds herself at odds with Caroline Bingley, played by Ted Lasso’s newest star Tanya Reynolds, who sees her as a rival in a dwindling marriage market.

The Other Bennet Sister struck a chord with audiences, recontextualizing characters from a beloved novel and giving a long-neglected figure her due. Mary’s constant pursuit of identity feels modern, despite the period setting. And with her family so often overlooking her, her ability to claim her own happiness feels like a true underdog story.

The Other Bennet Sister will show what comes after love and marriage in its upcoming three-episode Christmas special. BritBox released the trailer for the new installment, catching up with Mary as she struggles with her new identity as a married woman and the accompanying expectations. “As Mary Bennet, I’d often spoke my mind freely,” she says in the trailer, before adding she now feels “lost.” This backslide into insecurity comes as a shock to audiences who watched her work so diligently to become self-assured throughout Season 1. She’s not the only one feeling lost amid big life changes, with Mary’s frenemy Caroline Bingley seeking help ahead of giving birth to her first child.

Caroline isn’t the only returning character. The trailer shows not only Mrs. Bennet, but Mary reuniting with her sisters played by Poppy Gilbert, Maddie Close, Grace Hogg-Robinson, and Molly Wright. Mr. Ryder, Charlotte, and Varada Sethu as Ann Baxter are also set to return, with Nerys Amber Stocks joining as Lucy, Mary's new housemaid.

After the success of The Other Bennet Sister, BritBox announced it will apply the same treatment to other Jane Austen novels in its Austen Untold anthology. The Other Elliot Sister is up next, shifting the focus to Persuasion’s Elizabeth Elliot. Austen’s posthumously published final novel focused on Elizabeth’s younger sister Anne as she reconnected with her first love. Similarly told across 10 episodes, Quintrell is returning to adapt Hadlow’s upcoming novel of the same name.

Production on the series is expected to begin in 2027. “Elizabeth Elliot is an intriguing figure at the edges of Persuasion - someone we know just enough about to wonder what might be going on beneath the surface,” Jane Tranter, CEO of Bad Wolf, explained in a press release. “We’re delighted to be returning to the world of Jane Austen with the BBC and BritBox, and to bring another overlooked character to the centre of her own story as part of Austen Untold - an exciting new anthology that gives us the chance to explore Austen’s world through the eyes of characters whose stories have yet to be fully explored.”

There's currently a renewed interest in the works of Jane Austen, with the recently released film adaptation of Sense and Sensibility and Netflix's upcoming Pride & Prejudice miniseries. So now is the perfect time to binge The Other Bennet Sister, especially with its upcoming Christmas special just weeks away. The feel-good show will only take five hours to watch, so it is perfect for a weekend or even a long night in. And it’s just the start, with BritBox promising more stories centering Austen's overlooked characters.

An unusual period drama heroine navigates societal expectations on a journey to London from Meryton in Regency-era England.

#3349. Michael B. Jordan's Involvement In New Prime Video Boxing Series Clarified By Creator

EXCLUSIVE: The Greatest creator has cleared up how involved Michael B. Jordan was in the making of the new boxing series.

Earlier this month, The Greatest premiered on Prime Video, chronicling the life of heavyweight icon Muhammad Ali. While Jaalen Best performed the man originally named Cassius Clay, Jordan, who has experience playing a boxer character thanks to the Creed movies, worked behind the scenes as an executive producer. Ben Watkins, who created The Greatest, opened up about how the Adonis Creed actor contributed to the series.

In an interview with ScreenRant's Brandon Zachary, Watkins recalled how Jordan was already a producer on The Greatest when he came aboard. The two men had “crossed paths many times before” and previously worked together on Burn Notice, though when the time came down for them to meet and discuss Watkins’ “approach” to The Greatest, it had “been a while” since they last talked. Regardless, Jordan was immediately receptive to Watkins’ ideas and promised that he would “protect” his “vision for the show,” feeling that “there was nobody else who could tell the story.” The showrunner continued:

That started our journey once I joined, and then the second time was when there was a moment where this show was on the fence about whether it was going to get greenlit or not. We knew we had a big meeting coming up with Prime Video executives, and we had a great presentation planned. We touched base with Mike, and he knew it was coming, and he was in the middle of a press tour or in production. Whatever was happening, he dropped everything and came to L.A. so he could be in that meeting in person and help seal the deal. Then we had a green light.

Then the bigger stuff was the support over time as a producer. He couldn't be in the trenches with us because he had so much else going on, but he could weigh in at very key times, and if it's push a button here, nudge something here, do this email, it was just really great to have someone like that. I've had really powerful entities in projects before, but I haven't had one that really put their ego to the side and said, 'What's best for the project? I know at this point I'm one of the biggest stars in the world, but what I'm right here right now is just this producer on this show trying to help you get your vision realized.’

While Jordan is best known for his roles in movies and TV shows like Friday Night Lights, Parenthood, Black Panther, Just Mercy, Without Remorse, and Sinners, he also has a sizable amount of producing credits on his resume. That includes TV shows like Gen:Lock, Raising Dion, and 61st Street, though like the latter series, he doesn’t appear on camera in The Greatest. As Watkins laid out, while Jordan couldn’t contribute to the Prime Video TV show on a day-to-day basis, he was nonetheless instrumental in making sure that the project turned out just the way Watkins wanted.

Michael B. Jordan has been a part of two franchises that have had critical and commercial success and in between, he's had fantastic smaller roles.

Best is joined in The Greatest’s main cast by Omari Hardwick as Cassius Clay Sr. Dana Gourrier as Odessa Clay, Kai Parham as Rahaman Ali, Giovanni Ribisi as Angelo Dundee, and Amin Joseph as Sonny Liston. The series has earned primarily positive critical reception, boasting an 85% Tomatometer on Rotten Tomatoes based off 20 reviews. Watkins also shared his hope that The Greatest will return for two more seasons to explore other chapters of Ali’s life.

The Greatest season 1 can be streamed in its entirety on Prime Video. Jordan will next be seen starring in The Thomas Crown Affair, which he also directed and executive produced, and releases in theaters on March 5, 2027.

#3348. ‘I Play Rocky’ Star P.J. Byrne Isn’t a Scene-Stealer — He’s Something Better

You might not always remember his name, but you know P.J. Byrne. A master of “hey, I love that guy!” roles, the actor is often classified as a scene-stealer, thanks to standout turns in everything from “The Wolf of Wall Street” and “Babylon” to “Coyote vs. Acme” and “The Rainmaker.”

Byrne is funny, yes, but also energetic and an eager scene partner. He improves his projects not by simply showing up and grabbing some quick guffaws, but by really doing the work, learning his characters inside and out, and making it a priority to truly understand his directors. In his own words, he’s not stealing scenes; he’s elevating them. He doesn’t ever want to be the best thing in a film or show — he wants his process to help everything be better. Related Stories ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott’s Towering Performance as a Dying Actor Can’t Overcome AIDS-Movie Awards Bait Clichés Jim Cummings Wakes Up to a Post-One-Night-Stand Crisis in ‘DISC’ — Watch the Short

He brings that same approach and ethic to his latest turn as iconic super-producer Irwin Winkler in Peter Farrelly’s crowd-pleasing semi-biopic “I Play Rocky.” Farrelly’s film tracks the “only in Hollywood!” making of Sylvester Stallone’s smash hit “Rocky,” a true underdog story that hinges on the constant rejection of the then-unknown star, who was intent on starring in the film he had written. Stallone’s quest is aided by the support of Winkler and his partner Robert Chartoff (also an excellent Toby Kebbell), who went so far as to mortgage their own homes to make “Rocky” a reality.

Well, it paid off — for both the eventual Best Picture winner “Rocky” and Farrelly’s own film, which also features a massive star turn from Anthony Ippolito as Sly. Sure, there’s lots of drama in the film (Stallone’s physical toll stands out), but Byrne consistently brings his signature good humor and big laughs to Winkler, without ever making the Hollywood icon feel too big or crazy for this particular story.

“For me, it’s actually the most grounded performance I’ve ever had, but — wildly! — getting some of the biggest laughs of my career,” Byrne told IndieWire during a recent interview. That’s the product of a process Byrne has worked on for decades. But as seems to be the case with an actor who is just as gregarious and charming in an interview as you’d expect, it’s also because of the collaborations that really get him excited. That’s better than scene-stealing.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: You’re the kind of performer that, when you show up in a project, I’m like, “Oh, my God, I’m so excited to see him!” You steal scenes by making them better. You’re not chewing the scenery, you’re not stomping in, but you are adding this extra oomph to everything.

P.J. Byrne: I really believe all ships rise with the tide. If someone hogs the scene, or they want to get all the hits, it just goes south. I’ve just been doing this so long now, and it’s been my 10,000 hours. It started when Mike Nichols saw me and was like, “You need to go do whatever you want” [in “Charlie Wilson’s War”]. That gave me the fearlessness with Marty to make up my own monologue for [“The Wolf of Wall Street”] and just go crazy. I think all these great directors see, “You know what? He does the work.”

Before I start filming anything — and this sounds nuts — I try to show up two weeks before, and I literally just live in a hotel, almost to the point, I’m in my underwear, I’m getting food delivered, and I’m [looking at the script] like, “Where can I raise moments and how can I elevate this character and make this moment truly pop?” It’s not to win it from anyone else. I have to make sure it’s not trite, and it potentially could be zeitgeist-y, and it potentially is a tee-up for everybody else to do it. But I also know, if you’re going to improvise and add stuff, it has to be a nuclear weapon.

I always make the joke, my bio will be, “P.J. Byrne, Over the Shoulder, Out of Focus.” I know when the camera is coming to me. I know I get one shot. It better be a nuclear weapon, because then that gives me the freedom. Directors, like the Mike Nicholses or the Martys or the Damien Chazelles, they’re like, “Just go.” Peter was like, “Get the handcuffs off him. We’ve trust that he’s done the work and passed us knowing that character.” But it’s so important to me to take their vision, because after a while you realize what they really want, and then you can imbue your character perfectly into that and then share that with the other cast members. But that is a lot of work. It’s a crazy amount of work.

You cannot just show up on the day and be like, “Oh, here’s a line that I think that I can really put my signature on.”

Look, some people might have that gift. My gift is coming up with 10 amazing ones, calling friends, “Anything like that, whatever, how’s this one, whatever.” But don’t get me wrong, when the scenes happen, if you get one shot, I have my nuclear weapon. If we’re doing it a couple times, I’ve got four more to throw in the mix, and maybe the fourth wins. But that, to me, is the most fun on set. I’m so crazily prepared. I could still do probably all the lines of the movie now, or some of the [other movies] that I’ve done.

I did a small part in “Green Book,” and really, there are no small parts. I so believe that. Doing these small parts gets me into the world of all these people, and then that grows within that project, or I get a ton of repeat business. But that’s the best interview to ever do. It’s like, see me in action, see how I’m on the set, see what I can bring and try to elevate everybody. I’m never down, like a Friday night at 4:00 a.m., I’m still the Energizer Bunny. That’s a big part of me, because I just know it’s like we’re so lucky to be doing this. Then, I always say, “ABC,” always be classy. It’s so easy to be nice.

I know, it really is. And it makes you feel better. It doesn’t feel good to be a jerk or to be angry or to hold onto things.

It makes no sense to me. But if I see anyone sort of slacking, it makes me crazy, because I’m probably friends with the writer or whoever’s involved. They’ve put years of their lives into this. We don’t need any cancers. This is such a team effort. That’s why this movie in particular was so special, because everybody was there to crush.

The fact that Peter gave me this chance, and Rick Montgomery, I did a commercial with him years ago. They’re always like, “He needs a bigger part in a movie. P.J. needs a bigger shot.” Toby Emmerich, I did “Horrible Bosses” and “Final Destination 5” with him. They all were sort of rooting for me to finally get the shot. And because I had that, I saw it in Anthony. Anthony was getting his shot. It’s about giving Rocky a shot.

This film doesn’t work without you and Toby being an incredibly believable duo. How did you two build that bond?

Me, in this movie, is nothing without Toby. Anything positive is because of that beautiful, insanely good actor, the great Toby Kebbell. There’s so much truth. It’s an interesting thing when you show up at set like, “We have to have a 20-year relationship. I’ve just met you nine minutes ago, and action.” You know when you meet people, you’re like, “Oh, we’re going to be homies. We’re going to be friends forever”? We had a conscious effort of just looking at each other. I think it comes through. We’re having whole conversations just looking at each other, because that’s really what producers are. They don’t talk a lot. They just observe the world.

What did you know about this real story before you came on board?

All I really knew was that he demanded to play the part. I knew that what he was doing in his life, that he had no money. Those are the fundamentals. The crazy part to me is the fact that the studio wanted him to fail. We all know how hard it is to make movies, and when the studio is purposely waiting for you to die, essentially, that was an extraordinary moment. The fact that it turned out this way, with the insane low budget, and they’re doing one takes, and we find the Steadicam, thank God.

Did you know that the real guy showed up when we were doing the steps scene? The man that made that camera, Garrett Brown. When you watch football games and you see the cameras drop, he’s the camera master of making the Steadicam, and everything else. The shot you see in the movie of the girl running up the stairs, that is actual footage, that’s real footage of his wife from 50 years ago. And he’s from “Sesame Street!” It’s like, what a cute place for it to come from.

OK, so this is crazy. Let’s just say, I knew of him, because he produced “The Wolf of Wall Street.” I know the power of Irwin Winkler, because when we were doing scenes, and there’s a thousand people in a room, and it’s just craziness, Irwin Winkler walks on with Marty Scorsese and 1,000 people shut up. You’re just like, “Who’s this? What’s happened?” People are very quiet for Marty, but when those two were chatting on set, it was like 1,000 people are quiet. It’s like, “OK, that’s an interesting asset that this man has.”

When I knew this was coming, I was like, “I have to get a shot at this. I must.” Thank God, Peter and Rick, they’re like, “Put it down. Let’s go. Let’s see what you got, baby.” So then when I did get the part, Irwin said, “Come over to my house, and we’ll chat.” It’s like, “Oh, fuck.” I go over, and he lives in a mansion north of Sunset Boulevard, and he calls it “the house that Rocky built.” It is every magical thing that you can imagine. He’s so gracious, his wife’s lovely.

You go into this amazing old school office, and you’re just, “Can I write every script and take meetings and calls in this room?” What’s so intimidating is, everybody famous from 1960 to present day, there’s a picture of them on his wall with him staring at you while you’re like, “Hi, can I ask about…?” And then he has a film crew there doing a documentary, so they’re filming me asking him questions. It’s an intimidating thing, because he remembers 50 years ago like it’s 15 minutes ago.

I learned from our own interview with Anthony that, while Sly said for a while that he wasn’t involved, he actually met with Peter before the film was made. But Peter was like, “Can you not talk about this? We don’t want you to feel too involved.” And then he went too far to the loop.

Yes. Crazy. Crazy. Crazy. No, yeah, they both blessed it. They both blessed the script. It’s like they blessed us playing those parts separately.

When you are on set with someone like Anthony, who is about to have this massive breakout, what does it feel like for you?

This is super meta, it’s life imitating art. He’s just a kid from Long Island. You’ve got to remember, what is he, 24 when he’s auditioning? We’re shooting, he’s 25. Sylvester was 29, 30, doing this movie. He’s also a younger kid playing this part. He’s number one on the call sheet. This is his first gigantic movie. He’s got Tracy Letts and Matt Dillon, he’s got Peter Farrelly. So it’s very intimidating. This is the greatest part ever, where you have to do the thing of a real thing that happened in a movie.

But the fact that we are living, in the theme of Sylvester Stallone, let’s give somebody a chance, it played out through all of us. I say it all time, I’m so lucky to have been around extraordinary performances, like Leo in “Wolf of Wall Street.” Margot Robbie in “Babylon,” when they do the scene where she comes on the set, and she has to cry, and she does one tear and then two tears, that was real every time. You become an audience member. Even though you’re there and you’re saying your lines, a part of your brain is like, “We’re in the zone, it’s happening.” And that happened with Anthony.

At times, I felt like, “Did Sylvester Stallone travel through space and time and possess a 25-year-old kid’s body?” It’s so natural, and subtle, and soulful, and heartfelt. I would literally look at Peter, and I was like, “He is the greatest actor ever?” It can be an “SNL” performance; it could be a caricature; everybody does a version of him. And it wasn’t just that. It was soulful.

At what point did you realize this was going to become such a crowd-pleaser? I wasn’t at the TIFF premiere, but I went the next morning, and that screening was like being at a Super Bowl or something. Everyone was constantly clapping and cheering and yelling.

None of us thought it would be that. [The TIFF premiere] is the greatest viewing experience of watching a movie that I’m in that I’ve ever had. People are jumping up during the movie, screaming and missing lines because they’re clapping. That was the greatest thing. I was like, “They’ve got to watch it again!” The standing ovation at the end, they stayed up as we were walking on the stage. It was almost an out-of-body experience. It was pure and beautiful. And then, thank God, there were so many moments where I added stuff, but the moment that I didn’t know was going to get that big of a laugh was, you know when the boxing choreographer comes on?

I do. The best boxing choreographer in Hollywood!

That guy’s incredible, too, that guy is so sick. In the original scene, though, I didn’t come on where he gives me his jacket, we added that little thing: “Oh, I’ll take your jacket. … That was interesting.” Also, in that bit, my character, all he said is, “It’s a boxing movie.” I went to Peter, I was like, “There has to be something more, because at this point, he’s never boxed, he can’t box, Stephan [James, who plays Carl Weathers] can’t box.” I’m like, “Let me get the world’s greatest boxing choreographer,” because the job as a producer is to put out fires and lower risk.

I was so nervous about that night because it was the night before Thanksgiving. I know it was late shooting, so I’m like, “Am I going to add a whole bit here at the end of this goddamn thing?” But to Peter’s cred, he’s like, “Well, let’s see what you got.” All those little things that you add, it just shows, if you do the work, if you’re true to what the character is, you’re true to the essence of what the film is, moments like that happen.

If you prepare enough, you can make character choices that are informed. I hear this from a lot of performers: “If you know it enough, you have more freedom.”

But you have to have a director — and this is the big part — who is fearless. Meaning, again, Peter, Chazelle, Marty, Clint Eastwood. They’re just like, “This is what I’m doing. I know what I’m doing, and then I’m going to pass the keys to everybody.” When you have other people who are operating out of fear … they’re not wanting to be creative, everyone’s tight and tense, and you feel it on set, and there’s no room to grow or play. You’re just hitting speed bumps the whole way.

You are also in another movie this year that I love, “Coyote vs. Acme.”

We’re starting to see a push to have it recognized as an animated film, including at the Oscars.

Apparently, they’re technically allowed. It’s over 75 percent animation, so they are allowed to be put into that category.

What does that possibility feel like for you, after everything this film had to go through to even get released?

The director, Dave Green, is a legend. I lived this process with this beautiful human. He’s another one of the kindest, classiest people, the way he handled the whole process, always being calm in the storm. We all knew, and as we’re doing it, something special is happening. We can all feel it. He’s another guy who’s like, “Let P.J. run and [John] Cena go, let Will [Forte] go.” That was another big, important thing, just that this movie is out there.

But also the biggest part truly, in my heart, is Eric Bauza. He just passed away, and he was the nicest, warmest, loveliest human being you’ve ever met. I really believe he’s our generational talent for voiceovers. He is the guy of our moment. He was presenting an award at the 2024 Annie Awards — and the bulk of his income came through Warner Bros., that’s the bulk of this man’s income — and he was the first person, art over commerce, going, “Release ‘Coyote vs. Acme!’” Against the people that pay him!

Please, God, let this movie be nominated. The work, the music, the animation, there’s so many extraordinary things. To think that that was not going to see the light of day! The fact that the world loved it, it’s got 96 percent on Rotten Tomatoes. It’s just like, the world’s right. Every once in a while, the world is right.

Do you get recognized on the street? And if so, what do you get recognized for?

It’s like anything and everything. Sometimes, they’ll just be like, “You’re a great stand-up comic.” I’m like, “I don’t even know what that means. I’ve never done that before.” Sometimes people hear my voice, and they’re like, “Are you from that cartoon?” That stuff, God, it goes back years, too. I did a show 15 years ago called “The Game,” and if I’m in Atlanta, they’re like, “Let’s go. I hate you, but I love you!” People screaming at me. Sometimes it’s “Wolf.” Sometimes super cinephiles go crazy for “Babylon.” They go absolutely nuts, corner you. Anybody talking about me? I’m always happy. That means I’m working or doing something.

My last question is my favorite to ask of people who I feel like have already done so many different things: What have you not done yet that you really want to do?

God, I would love to do a “Hoosiers” and be a coach. No one’s putting me in a war movie, but if you look at it now, I’m kind of growing into the general role, or some higher officer role. I want to be a bad guy in “Star Wars.” I want to be like, “Let me see how someone spends $340 million.” I want to be the man in “Mission: Impossible” standing next to Tom Cruise, or being the other guy on a computer. All of the big massive movies, because I miss doing that stuff, and they don’t shoot in LA as much, those big monster, masterful movies.

Ultimately, I want to work with great directors who are fearless. That’s the real thing. The directors that go, “P.J., take the handcuffs off and go out there and play, let them throw the touchdown pass to you.” The quarterback’s the star, but I promise I will make a great play as the wide receiver. Whoever that person is, whoever’s doing that, I will show up, and I promise I will score for you.

An Amazon MGM Studios release, “I Play Rocky” will be in theaters everywhere on Friday, November 20.

#3346. iOS 27.3 gives Apple’s Calendar app new design updates

iOS 27.3 beta 2 arrived today, most notably giving the iPhone Duo a face unlock feature. The update also includes some design updates for Apple’s Calendar app.

When you open Apple’s Calendar app in iOS 27.3, the interface will look largely familiar to what was there before. But there are some key design changes that make the app better suited for one-handed use.

Most notably, the buttons for search and for adding a new event have both been moved from the top of the screen to the bottom.

This is a welcome change for anyone who uses their iPhone one-handed a lot, as both important buttons were previously in the top-right corner. I normally use my iPhone in my left hand, so they were especially hard to reach before.

Additionally, Apple has moved the current month to the top-center of the screen and added the year too. Because the year is now always prominently visible, Apple removed it from the back button in the top-left.

Finally, the ‘Today’ button that takes you back to the current day has been changed to always show the actual date. So right now, it reads ‘Mon 16.’

You can reference the full side-by-side in the image above. Overall, these are relatively minor changes but they could make a big difference in everyday use.

What do you think of Apple Calendar’s design updates in iOS 27.3? Let us know in the comments.

#3345. This Vizio Soundbar Comes With Wireless Surround Speakers, and It's Nearly 50% Off for Early Black Friday

Walmart’s early Black Friday sale just kicked off, offering no shortage of worthy tech deals, and one home audio deal in particular has our attention.  If you’re looking to level up your home theater audio setup for less, the Vizio 4.1 Pro SV410YW-10 Soundbar and wireless surround speakers setup with Dolby Atmos and DTS:X support is on sale for $79 (originally $148), a nearly 50% discount.

The two pre-paired wireless surround speakers can be positioned behind or beside your seating area, while two bass drivers built into the 32-inch soundbar mean you don’t need a separate subwoofer.  The system maxes out at 95 dB, with bass extending to 50 Hz.

The SV410YW-1 connects to your television through HDMI eARC and supports CEC, so you can adjust the volume with your TV remote. While its integrated subwoofers won’t give you the same impressive low end as a dedicated unit, this system still delivers robust, bassy sound that goes far beyond built-in TV speakers. There’s an added perk for Vizio TV owners—it can be attached directly beneath the screen using the QuickFit feature.

Along with the deal are additional promos, like up to two free months of Apple Music and up to a free month of Apple TV. If your current TV sound setup is lacking some oomph and you want an under-$100 upgrade with a subwoofer and soundbar, the Vizio 4.1 Pro SV410YW-10 Soundbar and wireless surround speaker combo is a good choice for the money.

#3344. 6 Superhero Movies From the 2020s That Are 10/10 Masterpieces

With how prominent superhero movies have been for decades upon decades, one would think they'd eventually slow down—but no, they're still going and stronger than ever. With some amazing superhero movies released thus far in the 2020s, and some of them being among the highest-grossing movies of all time, it's hard to believe that superhero films will be going anywhere anytime soon.

Whether they come from the land of Marvel or DC Comics, there have been some astounding superhero adventures audiences have gone on in this new decade. While it may not be over just yet, what viewers have been treated to so far is more than worth noting. There are been some truly excellent projects that one could easily consider 10/10 masterpieces in one way or another.

If there's a superhero movie that flew under the radar of most, it is 2023's Blue Beetle. Directed by the excellent Angel Manuel Soto, starring the ever-lovable Xolo Maridueña, Blue Beetle ended up being a movie that—for those who went out to see it—was critically well-received. The title almost feels like Sam Raimi's Spider-Man for the DC universe, and that's helped it become very memorable.

The story of Jaime Reyes is such a strong one, filled to the brim with relatability. Following the young man as he comes back from college and struggles to find a job to help his family, he eventually comes across the Scarab through a freak incident, and dons the powers of the titular Blue Beetle. It's a true coming-of-age story that is a great watch from minute one to the final second. In a time of multiversal superhero movies releasing yearly, the likes of a blockbuster superhero movie like Blue Beetle felt like a true breath of fresh air in 2023.

James Gunn is a great filmmaker—this much has been clear for quite some time—and the general audience really became acquainted with his work in 2014 with the release of Guardians of the Galaxy. This Marvel trilogy became what he would most prominently be known for quite some time—until he became the co-head of DC Studios a short time after. So, with the release of this trilogy-capper, people knew Gunn had to really knock it out of the park to impress the audience.

Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 is a great example of how to satisfyingly wrap up a trilogy, and give almost all of the primary characters a genuinely happy ending. Everyone gets a good conclusion to their character arcs, and it leaves the fans feeling like there's a true full-circle to the story that began in Guardians of the Galaxy. While he teases major deaths a good couple of times throughout the runtime, the Guardians all get a happy ending of some sort. When the standard for finales is typically leaving viewers with a heartbreaking death, getting to see these fan-favorites make their way out and end their journeys with a happy celebration is heartwarming.

Four powers, and four completely different kinds of person behind them. Here is what you would wake up with, what it would cost you, and why the MCU keeps handing it to somebody exactly like you.

You get the power that is really about taking the hit so that nobody else has to. Strength in the MCU always lands on people who were already carrying too much, which is exactly why it suits you.

You get the power that never switches off. Spider-sense is a gift and a nervous system on permanent alert, and the people who get it in these films are always the ones who were already worrying about everybody.

You get the quietest power in the building, and quietly the most useful. Invisibility comes with force fields for a reason, because the people who prefer not to be seen are usually the ones holding a shield around everybody else.

You get the biggest and least comfortable power on the list, the one that runs directly on feeling. Chaos magic is not really a superpower in the MCU so much as an emotional state with consequences attached.

For quite some time, Batman in cinema has been portrayed in a couple different ways, but not one that really hones in on his detective side (he's considered The World's Greatest Detective for a reason). Fans of the Big Bat finally were treated to a film that does just that in 2022, thanks to director Matt Reeves and superstar Robert Pattinson. The Batman is a crime noir that follows The Dark Knight in his second year as he attempts to solve the crimes of a new serial killer known simply as the Riddler (Paul Dano).

The Batman being so detective-focused is something that pleased a plethora of fans, and it allowed the story to be beyond engaging. Reeves' direction bleeds style and personality, making the movie feel one of a kind, and like a Gotham City that audiences have never experienced in previous Batman media. Pattinson does a stellar job bringing this loner hero to life in a way that truly gives him an amazing duality.

It's safe to say that the 2020s have treated James Gunn pretty well (until recently, that is). Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 isn't the only smash hit he got to have in the 2020s. Another one of his best comes in the form of DC's The Suicide Squad. No one could have ever expected him to bring this franchise out from the grave it was exiled to after Suicide Squad, but he did.

This 2021 title is not only hilarious and visually vibrant, but has such a distinct heart and soul at the center of it. Much like Guardians of the Galaxy, James took these misfits and turned them into fully fleshed out, three-dimensional characters that are so easy to fall in love with. Granted, he managed to make the Guardians of the Galaxy MCU fan-favorites, so this seems in line with his previous superhero movie track record.

If one were to ask almost anyone, they'd say that Spider-Man: Brand New Day is the Spider-Man movie that people have been waiting about a decade for. After the conclusion of the trilogy that began with Spider-Man: Homecoming, fans were happy, but craving something different—a more grounded, street-level Spider-Man story. That is exactly what Spider-Man: Brand New Day is.

This project is so phenomenal and beloved that it has quickly become one of the highest-grossing movies of all time—landing in the current top three. The new director, Destin Daniel Cretton (known for Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings), did an exceptional job taking all the issues people had with the previous movies, and improving on as many of them as he could. Not only that, but it acts as the official introduction to the MCU's Jean Grey (Sadie Sink), and does so in a manner that feels natural and unforced.

There's absolutely no denying that Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse's release in 2018 changed the film medium forever. So, when it came to getting a sequel, it was hard to believe they could create something that could live up to the immense legacy that the 2018 title set. But, come 2023, audiences would soon see that Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse more than lives up to the legacy of the first film.

This sequel takes everything people loved about the first and expands upon those things. New art styles are introduced for new Spider-People, an incredible cast comes together to bring these characters to life, the attention to detail is off the charts, and the screenplay exceeds expectations. It is a living and breathing trolley problem that tests the protagonists in every single scene. There's no question that the trilogy-capper, Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse, has a gargantuant mountain to climb when it comes to following this film up.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3343. Christopher Nolan and Guillermo del Toro Break Down ‘The Odyssey’ Monsters and AI’s Limitations with Production VFX Supervisor Andrew Jackson

With “The Odyssey,” Christopher Nolan ventured into the realm of fantasy for the first time, realizing a time of towering monsters, swirling whirlpools, and apparent magic. The production is a true showcase for his longtime collaborator, production visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson, who began working on the film‘s elaborate set pieces far ahead of production.

“What’s essential is having the visual effects team be part of the main unit through prep, through the shoot, everything — and not treating you guys as somebody that’s going to come on afterwards and add to the film,” Nolan said, speaking with Jackson during a panel following a Visual Effects Society screening of “The Odyssey” at the IMAX auditorium of AMC Theatres’ Universal Cinema location in Los Angeles. The discussion was moderated by Guillermo del Toro. Related Stories ‘I Play Rocky’ Star P.J. Byrne Isn’t a Scene-Stealer — He’s Something Better ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott’s Towering Performance as a Dying Actor Can’t Overcome AIDS-Movie Awards Bait Clichés

“What I’ve found through the years is to treat the effects as a remedial thing that is separate from everything is a big mistake,” del Toro added. “The beauty of it and the respect for the crafts is to integrate them early enough so that they are part of a physical solution as well as the post-production solution.”

The panel offered a detailed breakdown of several standout sequences in “The Odyssey,” including the early encounter with the Cyclops, which was realized with a mix of animatronic puppetry, digital effects, and a performance by clowning veteran Bill Irwin. Nolan shared that Jackson, who started as a model maker, is always one of his earliest collaborators — he was the first person to read the script for “Oppenheimer,” even. Integrating the various design elements of the Cyclops required a constant conversation from pre-production through the editing room.

“We were forced to shorten the time we had to build it,” Jackson began. Nolan then offered a joke: “I like the word forced. It’s good. I’m getting used to my crew members just vilifying me completely as we sit in these Q&As.”

“We both know that the result of being forced to trim away all the more complex parts of the plan resulted in a solution that was better than it would’ve been if we had continued with the original plan,” Jackson continued. “We basically just made a very, very simple marionette, which had still detailed solid components for the physical body, but just missed out on all the complicated joints and where the parts intersected. But the fact that it was simple and moved in a fascinating way that had a life of its own became really compelling.”

“I knew that one day you’d be sitting here and Guillermo del Toro would say it was perfectly integrated, so it’s all worth it,” Nolan said.

As with many industry Q&As these days, the topic of artificial intelligence’s impact on the filmmaking process, particularly on the field of visual effects, was addressed. Nolan, Jackson, and del Toro each emphasized the need for human oversight of the technology’s implementation, suggesting that “The Odyssey” could not have been realized without the conversations that happened across the film’s various departments.

“In an age with artificial intelligence looming — with synthetic creativity around us, or whatever — it’s actually very important to acknowledge the artistry that goes into the compositing process,” Nolan said. “My demand on the compositors and the animators is always to be using their eye rather than their brain, if you like, rather than simulating things or creating a simulation reality. I want them to look at it with an artist’s eye: the way matte painters who were working on glass paintings did, so that there’s an impressionistic quality in the composites.”

“The defense of the human touch and the defense of the craft is as urgent, if not more urgent, to VFX because it is the one that has gotten assailed the fastest by things like AI, which was not invented or demanded from any artist,” del Toro said. “It was demanded and created by people that were alien to that and appeal only to time and money mostly.”

“Well, time and money and also a misunderstanding of the process,” Nolan said.

“You’re absolutely going to need artists to know even whether the new tools have delivered things that you want. You need people to be able to assess that,” Jackson said.

#3342. macOS 27.3 beta 2 now available with vertical tabs in Safari, native Live Activities, more

Apple is rolling out the second developer beta of macOS 27.3 ahead of the official launch of the update, which includes several notable additions. Here’s what’s coming.

Two weeks ago, Apple released macOS 27.3 developer beta 1, followed by the public beta a few days later, amid a slew of hardware releases that included new M6-powered iMacs and 14-inch MacBook Pro, and the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

And contrary to macOS 27.2, the new update is shaping up to be pretty significant. In addition to expanding Siri AI support to four more languages, including Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese, the system also expands Siri AI’s capabilities across Apple’s own apps, allowing users to perform more complex actions in apps like Messages, Music, Calendar, Photos, and Reminders, as well as manage files and folders.

Apple is also introducing new tools for third-party developers to create advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions, allowing the assistant to coordinate multistep actions across different apps.

macOS 27.3 also introduces Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari, as well as native Live Activities support in the menu bar. Additionally, macOS 27.3 so far include native Markdown rendering in Quick Look, a new Pro Light screensaver, and additional checks for potentially harmful content shared through public iCloud links.

The build number for macOS 27.3 Golden Gate developer beta 2 is 26C5047e. We are digging through the system and will report back with what we find.
